Because six teams share four large convection ovens, oven slots are staggered every ten minutes. Your team's assigned baking window is printed on the badge you will receive at 9:30 a.m. check-in.

Good luck to all bakers!

items.prompt: According to acoustic researchers, what kind of sound disrupts patients' sleep the most?
choices: Rain tapping gently outside a closed window.
Sudden sharp noise peaks such as a cart hitting a floor seam.
Quiet classical music in the lobby.
items.explanation: sudden peaks in sound disturb sleep far more than a low, steady hum（低い一定音より突発的な鋭いピーク音）。
distractorReasons: 一定の低い音より突発音のほうが妨げる。
窓の外の優しい雨音ではない。
第2段落の説明と一致。
ロビーの静かな音楽ではない。
items.translation: 音響研究者によると、患者の睡眠を最も妨げるのはどのような音ですか。

passage.title: How Quiet Floors Help Hospital Patients Recover
passage.text:
When patients stay overnight in a hospital, uninterrupted sleep is one of the strongest aids to healing. Ironically, hospital wards have long been among the hardest places to sleep soundly. Alongside necessary medical monitors, everyday corridor sounds—squeaking supply carts, echoing footsteps on hard vinyl tiles, and clicking door latches—repeatedly wake light sleepers.

Acoustic researchers measuring ward noise found that sudden peaks in sound disturb sleep far more than a low, steady hum. A metal cart rolling over a tiny seam in a hard floor can send a sharp sixty-five-decibel clatter into nearby rooms, raising a sleeping patient's heart rate even if the person does not fully remember waking up.

To tackle this problem without sacrificing hygiene, hospital designers have rethought flooring and hardware from the ground up. New rubber-composite floors cushion footsteps and cart wheels while remaining seamless and easy to disinfect—unlike carpets, which trap dust and spills. Equally simple mechanical changes help: replacing metal trash-can lids with slow-closing dampers and fitting supply carts with soft polyurethane casters cut corridor noise spikes nearly in half during pilot studies.

Staff well-being improves alongside patient rest. Nurses walking ten kilometers per shift on cushioned rubber floors report less knee and back fatigue, and quieter hallways reduce misunderstandings when doctors discuss medication doses.

Thoughtful hospital design recognizes that recovery depends not only on advanced medicine, but also on a calm sensory environment.
passage.translation: 入院患者にとって途切れない睡眠は回復を助ける大きな力ですが、皮肉なことに病棟は長く熟睡しにくい場所でした。医療モニターだけでなく、廊下を通るワゴンのきしみ、硬いビニール床に響く足音、ドアの金具のカチッという音が眠りの浅い患者を何度も起こしてしまうのです。病棟の騒音を調べた音響研究者によると、低い一定の音よりも突発的な鋭い音のほうがはるかに睡眠を妨げ、床の継ぎ目を金属ワゴンが越える65デシベルの衝撃音は本人が目覚めた記憶がなくても心拍数を跳ね上げます。衛生面を損なわずにこれを解決するため、清掃・消毒しやすく継ぎ目のないゴム複合床材で足音や車輪の振動を吸収したり、ごみ箱のふたに静音ダンパーをつけワゴンの車輪を柔らかいポリウレタン製に替えたりする工夫が広がり、試験導入では廊下の突発音がほぼ半減しました。1勤務で10キロ歩く看護師の膝や腰の疲れも減り、投薬量の聞き間違いも減るなど、穏やかな音環境は患者と医療スタッフの双方を支えています。

items.prompt: Why don't hospitals simply lay ordinary carpet in ward corridors?
choices: Carpets make footsteps three times louder.
Carpet fibers interfere with X-ray machines.
Nurses cannot push wheelchairs on any soft surface.
Carpets trap dust and spills, making strict disinfection difficult.
items.explanation: unlike carpets, which trap dust and spills（カーペットはほこりやこぼれた液体をため込み消毒しにくい）。
distractorReasons: 足音が3倍大きくなることはない。
X線干渉の話はない。
ゴム複合床の上ではカートも問題なく動かせる。
第3段落の衛生上の理由と一致。
items.translation: 病院が病棟の廊下に普通のカーペットを敷かないのはなぜですか。

Giving every patient loud ear headphones.

大音量ヘッドホン配布ではない。
items.translation: 廊下の突発的な騒音をほぼ半減させるのに役立った簡単な設備変更は何ですか。

カルテ記入不要ではない。
第4段落の2つの利点と一致。
正午の消灯ではない。
items.translation: クッション性のあるゴム床と静かな廊下は医療スタッフにどのような恩恵をもたらしますか。

items.prompt: The city council voted to (     ) the old brick warehouse into a youth art gallery.
items.explanation: convert A into Bで「AをBに改装する・転換する」。古いレンガ倉庫をギャラリーに変える。
distractorReasons: complainは苦情を言う。
confuseは混乱させる。
competeは競争する。
convert ... into ~ で〜に作り変える。
items.translation: 市議会は古いレンガ造りの倉庫を青少年アートギャラリーに改装することを可決しました。

items.prompt: You can borrow up to six magazines at a time free of (     ) with a student card.
items.explanation: free of chargeで「無料で」。学生証があれば一度に6冊まで無料。
distractorReasons: changeはお釣り・変化。
free of chargeで無料で。
chanceは機会。
choiceは選択。
items.translation: 学生証があれば、無料で一度に雑誌を6冊まで借りられます。

items.prompt: Because the morning bus was delayed, I barely made it to school (     ) time.
items.explanation: on timeで「時間どおりに・始業時刻に遅れずに」（in timeと迷わぬようonのみ配置）。
distractorReasons: at timeとは言わない。
by timeとは言わない。
make it ... on timeで定刻に間に合う。
of timeとは言わない。
items.translation: 朝のバスが遅れたため、私はかろうじて始業時刻どおりに学校へ着きました。

items.prompt: This stainless-steel thermos keeps soup (     ) hot for more than six hours.
items.explanation: piping hotで料理や飲み物が「熱々の・湯気が立つほど熱い」。
distractorReasons: piping hotで熱々の。
pouringは土砂降りの（rain）。
pullingは引く。
pointingは指さす。
items.translation: このステンレス製保温ポットは6時間以上スープを熱々に保ちます。

items.prompt: Ms. Kudo congratulated the choir members (     ) winning the gold prize.
items.explanation: congratulate＋人＋on doingで「〜したことで（人）を祝福する」。
distractorReasons: ofは使わない。
toは使わない。
atは使わない。
congratulate ... on ~ で〜を祝う。
items.translation: 工藤先生は金賞を受賞した合唱部員たちを祝福しました。

items.prompt: There is no (     ) trying to dry thick jeans outdoors on such a humid day.
items.explanation: There is no point (in) doingで「〜しても無駄である・意味がない」。
distractorReasons: There is no point tryingで試みても意味がない。
placeは場所。
partは部分。
priceは価格。
items.translation: こんなに湿度の高い日に厚手のジーンズを外で乾かそうとしても無駄です。

items.prompt: The hiking club set (     ) from the mountain hut just as the sun rose.
items.explanation: set out from ... で「…から出発する」。日の出とともに山小屋を出発した。
distractorReasons: set inは（雨季や寒さが）始まる。
set outで出発する。
set downは書き留める・下ろす。
set backは遅らせる。
items.translation: 登山部はちょうど日が昇ったときに山小屋を出発しました。

items.prompt: My laptop battery needs (     ) because it runs out in less than forty minutes.
items.explanation: 物が主語でneed＋動名詞（replacing）は「交換される必要がある（＝need to be replaced）」。
distractorReasons: 原形は置けない。
過去分詞単独は標準英語では置かない。
needs replacingで交換が必要だ。
to replaceだと能動になり目的語が欠ける。
items.translation: 40分もたたずに切れてしまうので、私のノートパソコンのバッテリーは交換が必要です。

items.prompt: Scarcely had the ferry left the harbor (     ) playful dolphins appeared beside the bow.
items.explanation: Scarcely had S＋過去分詞 ... when ~ で「…するやいなや〜した」。
distractorReasons: thanはNo soonerと組む。
Scarcely ... when ~ の定型。
asは使わない。
thatは使わない。
items.translation: フェリーが港を出るやいなや、遊び好きなイルカが船首の横に姿を現しました。

items.prompt: From my point of (     ), building a bicycle lane is safer than widening the road.
items.explanation: from one's point of viewで「〜の観点からは・私の考えでは」。
distractorReasons: lookは見た目。
sightは視界。

passage.title: Why Coastal Towns Paint Lighthouses in Distinct Stripes
passage.text:
Postcards of seacoasts often show a tall white lighthouse standing on a rocky headland. Travel along an actual coastline, however, and you quickly notice that neighboring lighthouses rarely look identical: one wears bold red-and-white horizontal bands, another spirals like a black-and-white barber pole, and a third is painted solid yellow.

At night, sailors identify lighthouses by their unique flash rhythm—for instance, two quick flashes every ten seconds. During daylight hours, however, a flashing lamp is hard to spot against bright sky or sea glare. Before satellite navigation existed, captains steering along a foggy coast with binoculars needed an unmistakable visual daytime marker, known to mariners as a "daymark." Giving adjacent towers contrasting patterns ensured that (21).

Background scenery also guides color choice. A pure white tower stands out sharply against dark pine forests, yet vanishes against chalk cliffs or winter snowdrifts, where red bands remain vivid. Even today, when ships carry digital chart plotters, maritime authorities maintain these painted daymarks as (22) whenever electronics fail at sea.
passage.translation: 海岸の絵葉書には岩場に立つ白い灯台がよく描かれますが、実際の海岸線を巡ると隣り合う灯台が同じ見た目をしていることはめったにありません。赤白の横縞、黒白のらせん模様、鮮やかな黄色一色など実に多彩です。夜間は「10秒ごとに2回点滅」といった固有の光の周期で灯台を見分けますが、昼間の明るい空や海面の照り返しの中では点滅光が見えにくくなります。衛星航法がなかった時代、霧がちな沿岸を双眼鏡で進む船長には昼間の確実な目印（昼標＝デイマーク）が必要であり、隣り合う塔に異なる模様を与えることで(21)ようにしたのです。また暗い松林の前では真っ白な塔が映えますが、白い崖や積雪の前では溶け込んでしまうため赤い帯が威力を発揮します。電子海図が普及した現在も、海上で電子機器が故障したときの(22)としてこれらの塗装が維持されています。

passage.title: Preparing Bicycles for the Lake Charity Ride
passage.text:
From: Lake Aoi Charity Ride Committee
To: Youth Category Riders
Subject: Helmet labels and water-station rules for Sunday

Dear riders,
Only five days remain until our 30-kilometer Lake Aoi Charity Ride! The weather outlook for Sunday is mild and dry, with light morning wind.

When you pick up your rider packet on Saturday afternoon (1:00 p.m. – 5:00 p.m. at Lakeshore Park Tent A), you will receive two matching number stickers: place the small sticker on the front of your helmet and wrap the long sticker around your seat post so marshals can record your checkpoint times.

To keep plastic waste off the lakeshore, our three rest stations will not hand out disposable paper or plastic cups. Instead, volunteers will refill riders' own bicycle water bottles from chilled tanks, along with sliced bananas and salt candies. Please arrive at the start corral by 8:15 a.m. with a full bottle.

Ride safely and enjoy the lake views!
Event Committee
passage.translation: あおい湖チャリティーライド実行委員会からユース部門参加者へのメール。日曜の30キロ走行まであと5日となり、当日は穏やかな晴天で朝風も弱い見込み。土曜午後1時〜5時に湖畔公園テントAで参加キットを受け取る際、同じ番号のシールが2枚入っているので、小さい方はヘルメット前面に貼り、細長い方はチェックポイント通過時刻の記録用にシートポストへ巻きつけること。湖畔のごみを減らすため3か所のエイドステーションでは使い捨てコップを配布せず、冷水タンクから各自の自転車用ボトルに給水し、カットバナナと塩飴を配る。ボトルを満タンにして午前8時15分までにスタート整列エリアへ集合すること。

passage.title: Why Old Bridges Were Built with Roofs
passage.text:
Travel through rural valleys in Switzerland, Austria, North America, or parts of Japan, and you may cross a wooden bridge that looks remarkably like a long narrow barn floating above a river. Tourists often assume the roof and side walls were added so travelers and horses could stay dry during sudden storms—or so nervous farm animals would not fear the rushing water below.

While shelter was a pleasant bonus, carpenters of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries had a much more practical structural reason: protecting the heavy timber trusses underneath from rot. An uncovered wooden bridge exposed to rain, snow, and summer sun typically needed major replacement within fifteen to twenty years. Water seeped into joints where beams met, froze and expanded in winter, and invited wood-eating fungi.

Adding a lightweight roof and shingle siding cost extra lumber at the start, yet shielded the load-bearing beams from moisture. When minor roof shingles wore out, villagers could replace them cheaply without closing the bridge or rebuilding its main frame. Protected this way, many covered timber bridges lasted eighty to over a hundred years—four or five times longer than open wooden spans.

When affordable steel and reinforced concrete arrived in the twentieth century, engineers no longer needed roofs to weatherproof bridges. Nevertheless, communities that preserved historic covered bridges have gained unexpected value: calm pedestrian crossings, local landmarks, and living lessons in resource-saving craftsmanship.

Sometimes the smartest way to make a structure endure is not choosing a rarer material, but keeping everyday weather off its bones.
passage.translation: スイスやオーストリア、北米、日本の一部などの山あいを旅すると、川の上に細長い納屋が浮かんでいるような屋根付き木橋に出会うことがあります。観光客は旅人や馬が雨宿りするため、あるいは家畜が川面を怖がらないために屋根や壁をつけたと考えがちです。確かに雨よけの利点はありましたが、18〜19世紀の大工が屋根を架けた最大の構造的理由は、橋を支える太い木組み（トラス）を腐食から守ることでした。雨雪と日差しにさらされる屋根なしの木橋は継ぎ目に水が染み込み、冬の凍結膨張や木材腐朽菌によって15〜20年で大規模な架け替えが必要になりました。軽い屋根と板壁を付ければ初期の木材は増えるものの主構造を湿気から守れ、傷んだ屋根板だけを安く張り替えることで80〜100年以上、つまり4〜5倍も長持ちしたのです。20世紀に鉄鋼や鉄筋コンクリートが普及して耐候用の屋根は不要になりましたが、保存された屋根付き橋は今も地域の象徴や省資源の知恵を伝える財産となっています。

passage.title: Why Bakeries Slash Bread Dough Before Baking
passage.text:
Look closely at a crusty French baguette or country loaf, and you will notice diagonal cuts running neatly across the golden top. Home bakers often assume these slashes—known professionally as "scoring"—are merely a baker's artistic signature. While distinct patterns do help identify different loaves, a sharp blade actually solves a basic physics problem inside a hot oven.

The moment raw dough hits a hot baking stone, yeast activity surges and trapped water turns into steam, causing the loaf to puff up rapidly during the first ten minutes. Meanwhile, dry oven heat quickly hardens the outer skin into a firm crust. If no cuts have been made, expanding gas pushes against the weakest random spot on the side or bottom, tearing an uneven blowout and leaving the interior dense in one half and hollow in the other. Scoring creates deliberate expansion joints so the loaf (21).

Angle and depth matter too. Holding the blade nearly flat creates a thin flap of dough that peels back into a crisp, caramelized ridge prized for flavor. Thus, a two-second cut just before baking controls both (22).
passage.translation: パリッとしたフランスパンやカンパーニュをよく見ると、黄金色の表面に斜めの切り込みがきれいに並んでいるのに気づきます。家庭でパンを焼く人は、専門用語で「クープ（スコア）」と呼ばれるこの切り込みを単なる職人の飾りサインだと思いがちですが、実は高温のオーブン内で起きる物理的な問題を解決しています。生の生地が熱い天板に触れた瞬間、酵母の働きが活発になり水分が水蒸気になって最初の10分間で急激に膨らみますが、同時に表面は熱で固い皮になります。切り込みがないと、膨張するガスが側面や底の弱い場所を不規則に突き破り、中身の詰まり方も偏ってしまいます。あらかじめ切り込みを入れることで生地が(21)ようにしているのです。刃を寝かせて入れると薄い縁がめくれて香ばしい焼き目も生まれ、焼成直前のわずか2秒のひと手間が(22)の両方を左右しています。

While distinct patterns do help identify different loaves, a sharp blade actually solves a basic physics problem inside a hot oven.

The moment raw dough hits a hot baking stone, yeast activity surges and trapped water turns into steam, causing the loaf to puff up rapidly during the first ten minutes. Meanwhile, dry oven heat quickly hardens the outer skin into a firm crust. If no cuts have been made, expanding gas pushes against the weakest random spot on the side or bottom, tearing an uneven blowout and leaving the interior dense in one half and hollow in the other. Scoring creates deliberate expansion joints so the loaf (21).

Angle and depth matter too. Holding the blade nearly flat creates a thin flap of dough that peels back into a crisp, caramelized ridge prized for flavor. Thus, a two-second cut just before baking controls both (22).

passage.title: Preparing for the Night Museum Tour
passage.text:
From: Education Desk, Prefectural Natural History Museum
To: Registered Families
Subject: Flashlight rules and check-in for Friday's "Fossils in the Dark" tour

Dear families,
We look forward to welcoming you to our special after-hours "Fossils in the Dark" tour this Friday! Exploring the dinosaur gallery with ceiling lights turned off lets everyone see dramatic shadows on tooth and claw textures that disappear under bright daytime lamps.

Check-in opens at the North Staff Entrance at 6:40 p.m. and closes promptly at 6:55 p.m., as the main glass doors lock automatically at seven. Please do NOT bring camping lanterns or ultra-bright bike headlights; our staff will lend every participant a narrow-beam red-filtered flashlight that protects night vision and prevents glare on glass cases.

Warm sweaters are recommended since air conditioning stays cool to protect specimens.

Museum Education Team

items.translation: 北側通用口での受付が午後6時55分で厳格に締め切られるのはなぜですか。

passage.title: How Pocket Parks Cool Busy Neighborhoods
passage.text:
When city governments talk about expanding green space, residents often picture sprawling central parks with boating ponds and long jogging loops. Finding ten empty hectares inside an already crowded district, however, is nearly impossible. Instead, urban planners from Tokyo to Madrid are turning tiny leftover plots—a vacant corner lot, a former gas station, or two unused parking spaces—into "pocket parks."

Measuring smaller than a tennis court, a single pocket park may hold just four shade trees, a permeable brick path, a drinking fountain, and three wooden benches. Modest as that sounds, grouping dozens of small green oases a five-minute walk apart changes how a neighborhood feels in summer. Tree canopies block direct solar heat on asphalt, while soil beds soak up sudden downpours that would otherwise flood storm drains.

Social researchers have noticed equally important human effects. Large destination parks require a planned weekend trip for elderly residents or parents with toddlers, whereas a bench beneath zelkova trees fifty meters from a grocery store invites spontaneous ten-minute rests every day. Regular eye contact among neighbors watering flower beds also builds informal community trust.

Maintaining thirty scattered mini-parks can stretch municipal gardening crews thin if handled centrally. Successful cities solve this by pairing public tree pruning with neighborhood "park friends" volunteers who sweep leaves, plant seasonal bulbs, and report broken lights.

Grand city parks remain irreplaceable treasures, yet weaving tiny green pockets into everyday streets proves that nature does not have to be huge to transform urban life.
passage.translation: 自治体が緑地の拡大を語るとき、池や長いジョギングコースを備えた広大な中央公園が思い浮かびがちですが、密集した市街地に10ヘクタールもの空き地を見つけるのはほぼ不可能です。そこで東京からマドリードまで都市計画者が進めているのが、角の空き地やガソリンスタンド跡、駐車場2台分の余剰空間などを活用する「ポケットパーク」です。テニスコートより小さな1か所に木が4本と透水性レンガの小道、水飲み場、ベンチ3脚があるだけでも、徒歩5分圏内に点在させることでアスファルトへの直射日光を遮り、急な豪雨を土に浸透させます。さらに遠出が必要な大型公園と違い、スーパーから50メートルのケヤキの木陰のベンチは高齢者や幼児連れが毎日気軽に10分休める場となり、花壇の手入れを通じた地域の信頼も育みます。分散管理の手間は行政の剪定と住民ボランティアの協働で補われており、小さな緑の網目が日常の街並みを変えています。

items.prompt: What two environmental benefits of pocket parks are mentioned in the second paragraph?

passage.title: Why Wooden Cutting Boards Stay Popular in Professional Kitchens
passage.text:
When smooth plastic cutting boards entered home kitchens decades ago, many cooks assumed traditional wooden boards would soon disappear. Plastic boards were light, inexpensive, and easy to load into hot dishwashers. Yet walk into bakeries, sushi counters, and restaurant prep rooms today, and thick end-grain boards made of hinoki cypress, maple, or ginkgo wood remain a chef's favorite surface.

Knife care is the first reason cooks stay loyal to wood. Hard glass, stone, or stiff plastic dulls a finely sharpened steel edge quickly because the blade slams into an unyielding surface on every chop. Wood fibers, particularly when arranged vertically like bristles on a brush, part slightly under the knife edge and spring back afterward. This gentle cushion lets chefs (21).

Food-safety experiments also surprised early skeptics. Deep knife grooves in old plastic boards can trap moisture and bacteria even after a quick wash, whereas dry natural wood pulls liquid droplets inward via capillary action, leaving surface microbes without the water they need to multiply. Provided cooks wash a wooden board promptly and stand it upright to dry, traditional timber offers (22).
passage.translation: 何十年か前に滑らかなプラスチック製のまな板が家庭の台所に普及したとき、多くの人は伝統的な木のまな板はやがて姿を消すだろうと考えました。プラスチック製は軽くて安価で食洗機にも入れやすかったからです。しかし今日のパン工房や寿司店、レストランの仕込み場をのぞけば、ヒノキやカエデ、イチョウで作られた厚い木のまな板が今も料理人に愛用されています。第1の理由は包丁への優しさです。ガラスや石、硬い樹脂は刃先が硬い面に毎回ぶつかってすぐ切れ味が落ちますが、木の繊維は刃を受け止めてわずかにしなり、料理人が(21)ようにしてくれます。また衛生面の実験でも、深い傷のついた古い樹脂製まな板には洗った後も水分と菌が残りやすい一方、乾いた天然木は毛細管現象で水滴を内部へ引き込み表面の菌の繁殖を抑えることが分かりました。使用後すぐに洗って立てて乾かせば、木のまな板は(22)を備えているのです。

passage.title: Notice About Locker Replacement in the Sports Center
passage.text:
From: Aoba Municipal Sports Center
To: Monthly Pass Holders
Subject: Empty rental lockers by May 28 for earthquake-latch upgrade

Dear pass holders,
To improve safety during earthquakes, the Sports Center will replace all 180 rental shoe and gear lockers on the first floor on Friday, May 29, and Saturday, May 30. The new steel lockers feature drop-proof latches that stay shut even during strong shaking.

If you currently rent a monthly locker, please take home all shoes, rackets, and toiletries before 9:00 p.m. on Thursday, May 28, and return your brass key to the front desk. Any items left inside on Friday morning will be packed in numbered bags and stored in the office for thirty days.

Your June rental fee will automatically be discounted by two days, and new wrist-band keys will be issued starting Sunday, May 31.

Sports Center Management
passage.translation: 青葉市民スポーツセンターから月極パス利用者へのメール。地震時の安全性向上のため、5月29日（金）・30日（土）に1階の月極レンタルロッカー全180台を入れ替える。新型スチールロッカーは強い揺れでも扉が開かない耐震ラッチを備える。現在契約中の利用者は5月28日（木）午後9時までに靴・ラケット・洗面用具をすべて持ち帰り、真鍮の鍵をフロントへ返却すること。金曜朝に残っていた荷物は番号付き袋に入れて事務室で30日間保管する。6月分の利用料からは2日分が自動割引され、5月31日（日）から新しいリストバンド式キーを交付する。

passage.title: How Sea Otters Help Underwater Kelp Forests Thrive
passage.text:
Along rocky Pacific coasts from northern Japan to Alaska and California, giant brown seaweeds called kelp grow upward from the seafloor like sunlit underwater forests. Towering strands of kelp shelter young rockfish, crabs, and sea snails while softening harsh winter waves before they strike coastal cliffs. Yet these lush underwater canopies depend surprisingly heavily on one furry marine mammal floating at the surface: the sea otter.

Unlike whales and seals, which rely on thick layers of blubber to stay warm in icy ocean water, sea otters have no blubber at all. Instead, they stay warm thanks to the densest fur in the animal kingdom AND a fast metabolism that requires eating roughly a quarter of their body weight in shellfish and sea urchins every single day.

That hearty appetite keeps the seafloor in balance. Spiny sea urchins graze on the root-like anchors that hold kelp stalks to rocks. When sea otters were hunted nearly to extinction for their pelts in the nineteenth century, sea urchin numbers exploded unchecked. Armies of urchins chewed through kelp anchors across miles of coast, turning rich underwater forests into bare rock "urchin barrens" where few fish could hide.

Where legal protection and conservation programs allowed sea otter populations to rebound in the late twentieth century, researchers watched a dramatic recovery unfold. By preying on exposed urchins, returning otters gave young kelp spores time to take hold and grow back into dense canopies—which in turn absorbed more dissolved carbon dioxide from coastal waters.

Studying otters, urchins, and kelp gave ecologists a classic example of a "keystone species": an animal whose everyday feeding habits quietly hold an entire ecosystem together.

passage.title: How Sea Otters Help Underwater Kelp Forests Thrive
passage.text:
Along rocky Pacific coasts from northern Japan to Alaska and California, giant brown seaweeds called kelp grow upward from the seafloor like sunlit underwater forests. Towering strands of kelp shelter young rockfish, crabs, and sea snails while softening harsh winter waves before they strike coastal cliffs. Yet these lush underwater canopies depend surprisingly heavily on one furry marine mammal floating at the surface: the sea otter.

Unlike whales and seals, which rely on thick layers of blubber to stay warm in icy ocean water, sea otters have no blubber at all. Instead, they stay warm thanks to the densest fur in the animal kingdom AND a fast metabolism that requires eating roughly a quarter of their body weight in shellfish and sea urchins every single day.

That hearty appetite keeps the seafloor in balance. Spiny sea urchins graze on the root-like anchors that hold kelp stalks to rocks. When sea otters were hunted nearly to extinction for their pelts in the nineteenth century, sea urchin numbers exploded unchecked. Armies of urchins chewed through kelp anchors across miles of coast, turning rich underwater forests into bare rock "urchin barrens" where few fish could hide.

Where legal protection and conservation programs allowed sea otter populations to rebound in the late twentieth century, researchers watched a dramatic recovery unfold. By preying on exposed urchins, returning otters gave young kelp spores time to take hold and grow back into dense canopies—which in turn absorbed more dissolved carbon dioxide from coastal waters.

Studying otters, urchins, and kelp gave ecologists a classic example of a "keystone species": an animal whose everyday feeding habits quietly hold an entire ecosystem together.

items.prompt: The librarian asked the boys to (     ) their voices near the study cubicles.

items.translation: 司書は学習ブースの近くでは声を小さくするよう男の子たちに頼みました。

distractorReasons: hourはこの接続詞句を作らない。
by the time ... で〜するまでには。
momentはthe moment S+V（〜するとすぐに）でbyと組まない。
periodも不可。
items.translation: 私たちが山頂に着いたころには、朝霧はすっかり晴れていました。

distractorReasons: contractは契約。
conflictは対立。
comfortは楽にすること・心地よさ。
conductは振る舞い。

without noticeで事前通告なしに。

a great manyは可算複数用。
a number ofも可算複数用。
severalも可算複数用。

distractorReasons: benefitはこの熟語を作らない。

profitも作らない。

stareはじっと見つめること。

passage.title: Why Passenger Airplanes Have Tiny Holes in Their Windows
passage.text:
Next time you settle into a window seat on a passenger jet, look near the bottom center of the clear pane: you will spot a tiny hole scarcely wider than a toothpick. Nervous flyers sometimes wonder whether the window is cracked, yet aerospace engineers call this feature a "bleed hole," and it is built into cabin windows on purpose.

A jetliner window actually consists of three separate layers of transparent acrylic resin. The thin inner pane facing your elbow is merely a protective scratch shield, whereas the thick outer pane bears the massive air-pressure difference between the thin atmosphere ten kilometers up and the pressurized passenger cabin. If both the outer and middle panes felt full cabin pressure all the time, both would suffer wear together. The tiny hole in the middle pane equalizes air pressure safely so that (21).

The bleed hole performs a neat everyday job too. Outside air at cruising altitude drops below minus fifty degrees Celsius. Allowing dry cabin air to circulate slowly between the panes prevents moisture from freezing onto the outer glass, ensuring passengers enjoy (22).
passage.translation: 今度旅客機の窓側席に座ったら、透明な窓の下部中央近くをよく見てみてください。つまようじほどの幅しかない小さな穴が見つかるはずです。ひび割れではないかと不安になる乗客もいますが、これは航空技術者が「ブリードホール（呼吸穴）」と呼ぶ意図的な設計です。旅客機の窓は実は3層のアクリル樹脂板でできており、ひじのすぐ横にある薄い内側の板は傷防止カバーにすぎず、分厚い外側の板が高度10キロの薄い外気と与圧された客室との大きな気圧差を受け止めています。もし外板と中板の両方に常に負荷がかかれば同時に摩耗してしまいますが、中板に小さな穴を開けて圧力を調整することで(21)ようになっています。また巡航高度の外気は氷点下50度以下になりますが、乾いた客室の空気を板の間に少しずつ通すことで凍結や曇りも防ぎ、乗客に(22)を届けています。

passage.title: Volunteer Shift Guide for the Town Marathon Water Station
passage.text:
From: Kawa-machi Marathon Organizing Committee
To: High School Volunteer Team (Station 3 – 10 km Mark)
Subject: How to hand cups smoothly to runners this Sunday

Dear Station 3 volunteers,
Thank you for helping staff the 10-kilometer water table for Sunday's Kawa-machi Half Marathon! Nearly 1,800 runners will pass our table between 9:25 a.m. and 10:30 a.m., so smooth teamwork will keep everyone safe.

Please fill paper cups only two-thirds full—full cups splash onto runners' shoes and make the asphalt slippery. When offering a cup, do NOT hold it tightly by the rim from below; instead, pinch the top edge lightly from the side with two fingers, call out "Water!" or "Sports drink!" clearly, and walk two steps forward alongside the runner as they grab it.

Wear waterproof sneakers and meet at the 10 km tent at 8:15 a.m. for table setup!

Organizing Committee
passage.translation: 川町マラソン実行委員会から10キロ地点第3給水所の高校生ボランティアへのメール。日曜のハーフマラソンでは午前9時25分〜10時30分の間に約1800人のランナーが通過する。紙コップに注ぐ量は3分の2までにすること（満杯だと靴にかかり路面が滑りやすくなる）。コップを渡す際はぎゅっと握りしめず、上端を横から2本指で軽くつまみ、「水です！」「スポーツドリンクです！」とはっきり声をかけながらランナーに合わせて2歩前に歩きつつ渡すこと。防水性のあるスニーカーを履き、午前8時15分に10キロ地点テントへ集合。

items.prompt: How should volunteers hold and hand a cup to an approaching runner?

第2段落後半の手順と完全一致。
3メートル先から投げるのではない。
items.translation: 近づいてくるランナーにどのようにコップを持って渡すべきですか。

passage.title: Why Botanical Illustrators Still Draw Plants by Hand
passage.text:
Modern smartphones and macro cameras can photograph an orchid petal in a fraction of a second, capturing millions of pixels of color. Given such effortless technology, visitors to natural history museums are often surprised to learn that botanists naming a newly discovered plant species still commission black-and-white pen-and-ink illustrations drawn by hand.

A single photograph, however sharp, shows only one individual plant at one moment in time. In the wild, a flower may bloom in April while its seed pod matures in August, or one leaf may be chewed by insects while a diagnostic root tuber stays hidden underground. Even worse, camera lenses struggle with depth of field at close range: focusing sharply on tiny pollen stamens blurs the stem hairs two centimeters behind them.

A trained botanical illustrator overcomes all of these limits on one sheet of paper. Consulting closely with the botanist—and often examining pressed herbarium specimens under a microscope—the artist combines buds, open blossoms, cross-sections of fruit, and magnified seed textures side by side in crystal-clear focus. Unnecessary shadows and distracting background leaves are omitted so another scientist a century later can verify the exact vein pattern that distinguishes the species from close relatives.

Digital tablets have certainly joined traditional crow-quill pens on many illustrators' desks, making revisions cleaner. Yet the core skill remains human observation rather than button-pressing: deciding which tiny details matter scientifically.

Far from competing, photography and hand illustration complement each other—photos record living color in habitat, while botanical line art preserves clear structural truth.
passage.translation: 現代のスマートフォンやマクロカメラは一瞬でランの花びらを何百万画素もの色彩で撮影できます。それにもかかわらず、新種の植物を記載する植物学者が今なお手描きの白黒ペン画（ボタニカル・イラストレーション）を専門家に依頼していると知ると、多くの人が驚きます。どれほど鮮明な写真も「ある瞬間の1個体」しか写せず、4月に咲く花と8月に熟す果実を同時には収められないうえ、接写ではピントの合う奥行が浅く雄しべに合わせると2センチ奥の茎の毛がぼけてしまいます。訓練を積んだ植物画家に顕微鏡観察や押し葉標本を組み合わせてもらえば、つぼみ・開花・果実の断面・種子の拡大図を1枚の紙の上にすべて鮮明なピントで並べ、紛らわしい影や背景を省いて近縁種と区別する葉脈の特徴を100年後の研究者にも正確に伝えられます。写真が生きた色彩を写し取る一方、手描きの線画は構造の真理を残す相補的な関係にあります。

passage.title: Why Teapots Have a Tiny Hole in the Lid
passage.text:
Pick up almost any ceramic or glass teapot, and you will spot a millimeter-wide pinhole pierced right through the lid beside the knob. First-time potters sometimes mistake it for a manufacturing flaw, yet leaving that tiny opening out turns pouring a simple cup of green tea into a messy struggle.

Imagine tipping a full teapot whose lid fits snugly with no vent at all. As tea begins flowing out of the narrow spout, the volume of air trapped above the hot water expands inside a sealed space, causing air pressure inside the pot to drop below the room's atmospheric pressure. Outside air then pushes back up through the spout itself, making the stream glug, sputter, and stop mid-pour—or worse, trapping steam pressure that pushes scalding water out unpredictably. Piercing a small vent in the lid lets outside air (21).

Experienced tea drinkers use that same hole as a control valve too. Pressing one finger lightly over the pinhole stops the flow instantly when a teacup is full, preventing drips on the tablecloth. Thus, one inconspicuous hole provides both (22).
passage.translation: 陶器やガラスの急須を手に取ると、つまみのすぐ横に直径数ミリの小さな穴が開いているのに気づきます。初めて陶芸をする人は不良品かと勘違いすることもありますが、この小さな穴がないと緑茶を1杯注ぐだけでも大変な苦労になります。空気穴のない密閉された蓋の急須を傾けたところを想像してみてください。細い注ぎ口からお茶が出始めると、ポット内部の空気の圧力が外気圧より下がり、外の空気が注ぎ口から逆流して「ゴボゴボ」と脈打ったり途中で止まったりしてしまいます。蓋に小さな通気孔を開けておくことで外の空気が(21)ようになるのです。さらに茶慣れた人は湯のみがいっぱいになった瞬間にこの穴を指先で軽く押さえてピタッと湯切れさせ、テーブルクロスへの垂れを防ぎます。目立たない1つの穴が(22)の両方をもたらしているのです。

passage.title: Instructions for the Astronomical Photo Contest
passage.text:
From: Youth Science Museum Contest Desk
To: High School Entrants
Subject: Raw file check and caption rules for "Night Sky Over My Town"

Dear entrants,
Thank you for registering for our annual "Night Sky Over My Town" student photography contest! Submissions close next Monday, October 19, at 8:00 p.m.

Each student may upload up to two photographs taken between January and October of this year. Basic adjustments to brightness and contrast are permitted, but pasting the moon from one photo onto a landscape from another—or using AI sky-replacement filters—will result in disqualification. Finalists will be asked to submit their unedited camera file to verify authenticity.

Please include the shooting date, town name, and exposure time in your caption, while leaving your own name and school off the image itself for blind judging.

Contest Secretariat
passage.translation: 青少年科学館コンテスト事務局から高校生応募者へのメール。「わが町の夜空」学生写真コンテストの応募締切は来週月曜10月19日午後8時。今年1月〜10月に撮影した写真を1人2点まで応募可能。明るさやコントラストの基本調整は可だが、別写真の月の合成やAI空置換フィルターの使用は失格となり、入賞候補者は真正性確認のため未編集の元データの提出を求められる。審査は匿名（ブラインド方式）で行うため、画像自体には氏名や学校名を入れず、キャプションに撮影日・市町村名・露光時間を記載すること。

So visitors never learn who won.
So judges can evaluate entries fairly without knowing who took them.

50文字超だからではない。
受賞者を永遠に隠すためではない。
撮影者名を伏せた公平なブラインド審査を行うため。

From: Youth Science Museum Contest Desk

Thank you for registering for our annual "Night Sky Over My Town" student photography contest! Submissions close next Monday, October 19, at 8:00 p.m.

Contest Secretariat

items.prompt: Why has more than seventy-five percent of traditional crop diversity disappeared from everyday farms?
choices: Supermarkets banned apples, potatoes, and tomatoes.
Commercial farming focused on a few uniform, high-yielding varieties suited for shipping.
Arctic glaciers covered seventy-five percent of farmland.
Insects ate every heirloom seed in 1920.
items.explanation: As commercial agriculture standardized around a handful of high-yielding hybrids for uniform shipping, however, more than seventy-five percent of traditional crop diversity vanishedとある。
distractorReasons: 販売禁止ではない。
第1段落後半の商業農業の品種集約の説明と一致。
氷河拡大ではない。
1920年の虫害全滅ではない。
items.translation: 伝統的な作物の多様性の75％以上が日常の農地から失われたのはなぜですか。

passage.title: How Seed Vaults Safeguard Future Crops
passage.text:
Walk down the vegetable aisle of a modern supermarket, and five or six glossy varieties of apples, potatoes, or tomatoes fill the bins. A century ago, regional farmers across the world grew thousands of local heirloom varieties—apples that ripened in frosty mountain valleys, rice strains tolerant of brackish coastal water, or beans resistant to specific soil beetles. As commercial agriculture standardized around a handful of high-yielding hybrids for uniform shipping, however, more than seventy-five percent of traditional crop diversity vanished from everyday fields.

Losing those obscure local seeds carries a serious hidden risk. When millions of hectares plant genetically identical crops, a single newly evolved fungus, insect pest, or severe heat wave can sweep across entire continents. Wild relatives and old village landraces often hold the exact genetic resistance plant breeders need to rescue vulnerable staples.

To prevent irreplaceable varieties from disappearing forever, agricultural scientists maintain over seventeen hundred national and regional "seed banks"—backed up by the famous Svalbard Global Seed Vault tunneled deep inside frozen Arctic rock in Norway. Harvested seeds are dried to low moisture, sealed inside foil packets at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, and periodically sprouted on test plots to refresh aging stock.

Yet cold vaults alone are not enough. Because climates and pests keep evolving in the real world, agronomists now partner with "living seed networks" of small farmers who continue planting heritage grains in local soil year after year, allowing crops to adapt naturally alongside cold-storage backups.
passage.translation: 現代のスーパーの青果売り場にはツヤのある5〜6品種のリンゴやジャガイモ、トマトが並んでいますが、1世紀前には霜の降りる谷で熟すリンゴや汽水に強い稲など何千もの在来品種が各地で育てられていました。輸送に適した少数の高収量品種への集約が進んだ結果、伝統的な作物の多様性の75％以上が畑から姿を消しました。この喪失には大きなリスクが潜んでいます。遺伝的に均一な作物が広大な面積に植えられると、新種のカビや害虫、猛暑が大陸規模で被害を広げかねず、そうした危機を救う耐性遺伝子は野生近縁種や古い地方品種に眠っていることが多いからです。かけがえのない品種の絶滅を防ぐため、ノルウェー北極圏の永久凍土に掘られたスヴァールバル世界種子貯蔵庫をはじめ世界に1700以上の種子バンクが整備され、乾燥させた種子を氷点下18度のアルミ袋で保管しています。さらに現実の気候や害虫の変化に合わせて作物が進化し続けられるよう、小規模農家が毎年畑で在来種を育て継ぐ「生きた種子ネットワーク」と冷凍保存を組み合わせる取り組みが広がっています。

items.prompt: Why is relying on genetically identical crops across vast areas risky?
choices: Farmers forget how to drive tractors.
Identical apples refuse to ripen in sunlight.
One new disease, pest, or extreme heat wave can devastate the entire crop at once.
Seeds turn into stones inside foil packets.
items.explanation: When millions of hectares plant genetically identical crops, a single newly evolved fungus, insect pest, or severe heat wave can sweep across entire continents.とある。
distractorReasons: トラクター運転忘れではない。
日光で熟さないからではない。
第2段落の単一品種リスクの説明と一致。
石に変わるのではない。
items.translation: 広大な面積で遺伝的に同一の作物ばかりに頼ることが危険なのはなぜですか。

items.prompt: How are seeds preserved inside facilities like the Svalbard Global Seed Vault?
choices: They are dried, sealed in foil packets, and stored at minus eighteen degrees Celsius.
They are boiled in saltwater and hung outdoors in summer.
They are planted under bright lamps inside ocean submarines.
They are mixed with fresh soil and watered every morning.
items.explanation: dried to low moisture, sealed inside foil packets at minus eighteen degrees Celsiusとある。
distractorReasons: 第3段落の低湿乾燥・アルミ袋密封・氷点下18度保管と一致。
塩水煮沸ではない。
潜水艦栽培ではない。
毎朝水やりすると発芽・腐敗してしまう。
items.translation: スヴァールバル世界種子貯蔵庫のような施設では、種子はどのように保存されていますか。

choices: Refrigerators in Norway cannot stay cold in winter.
Growing heritage crops in real fields lets them keep adapting to changing climates and pests.
Foil packets last only forty-eight hours.
Small farmers refuse to share seeds with scientists.
items.explanation: allowing crops to adapt naturally alongside cold-storage backups（変化する気候や害虫に畑で自然適応させ続けられるため）。

最終段落の冷凍保存と圃場栽培の相補的役割と一致。
48時間しか持たないとは逆。
共有拒否ではなく連携している（partner with）。
items.translation: 農学者が冷凍種子バンクと地域農家の「生きた種子ネットワーク」を組み合わせているのはなぜですか。

items.prompt: The city ferry can (     ) up to two hundred passengers and twelve cars.
items.explanation: 市営フェリーは乗客200人と車12台まで「収容できる」accommodate。
distractorReasons: exaggerateは誇張する。
hesitateはためらう。
accommodateは（定員・車両などを）収容する。
accelerateは加速する。
items.translation: その市営フェリーは最大で乗客200人と乗用車12台を乗せることができます。

items.prompt: On (     ) of heavy snowfall, all expressway buses bound for Nagano were suspended.
items.explanation: on account of ... で「…のために・…が理由で」。大雪のため長野行きの高速バスがすべて運休になった。
distractorReasons: on account ofで〜のために。
on behalf ofは〜を代表して。
on purposeはわざと（後ろにofをとらない）。
on averageは平均して。
items.translation: 大雪のため、長野行きの高速バスはすべて運休となりました。

items.prompt: Adding a pinch of salt brings out the natural (     ) of ripe watermelon.
items.explanation: ひとつまみの塩が熟したスイカの自然な「甘み」を引き立てるsweetness。
distractorReasons: shynessは内気さ。
sicknessは病気。
sharpnessは鋭さ。
sweetnessは甘さ。ripe watermelonと合致。
items.translation: ひとつまみの塩を加えると、熟したスイカ本来の甘みが引き立ちます。

items.prompt: To my (     ), the lost wallet still had every bill and train pass inside.
items.explanation: to one's reliefで「ほっとしたことに」。なくした財布にお札も定期券もすべて残っていて安心した。
distractorReasons: beliefは信念。
to my reliefで私が安心したことには。
griefは深い悲しみ（中身が無事だった文脈と逆）。
briefは概要。
items.translation: ほっとしたことに、なくした財布の中にはお札も定期券もすべてそのまま入っていました。

items.prompt: This stainless-steel mug keeps soup hot for six hours, (     ) of outside weather.
items.explanation: regardless of ... で「…にかかわらず」。外の天気にかかわらず6時間スープを温かく保つ。
distractorReasons: helplessは無力な。
carelessは不注意な。
regardless ofで〜に関係なく・かかわらず。
speechlessは言葉が出ない。
items.translation: このステンレスマグは外の天候にかかわらず、スープを6時間温かいまま保ちます。

items.prompt: Only a (     ) of tickets remained for Sunday's jazz concert.
items.explanation: a handful of ... で「ひと握りの・ごく少数の」。日曜のジャズコンサートのチケットはほんのわずかしか残っていなかった。
distractorReasons: armfulはひと抱え。
mouthfulは一口分。
spoonfulはひとさじ分。
only a handful of ticketsでごく少数のチケット。
items.translation: 日曜日のジャズコンサートのチケットは、ほんのわずかしか残っていませんでした。

items.prompt: Please take your belongings with you and leave nothing (     ) on the bus.
items.explanation: leave nothing behindで「忘れ物を何もしない（何も後に残さない）」。
distractorReasons: leave ... behindで置き忘れる・残していく。
besideは前置詞で目的語が必要。
beyondも前置詞。
beneathも下に。
items.translation: お手荷物はすべてお持ちになり、バス車内にお忘れ物のないようお願いします。

items.prompt: Having (     ) up in a port town, Mr. Sato predicts winds from cloud shapes.
items.explanation: 完了形の分詞構文Having＋過去分詞grown up（港町で育ったので）。
distractorReasons: 原形は不可。
Having grown upで育った経験があるため。
過去形は不可。
Having growingとは言わない。
items.translation: 港町で育ったため、佐藤さんは雲の形から風の変化を予測します。

items.prompt: Our club couldn't afford new uniforms; we made (     ) with repaired jerseys.
items.explanation: make do with ... で「（手持ちの物で）間に合わせる・やりくりする」。補修したユニフォームで間に合わせた。
distractorReasons: make do withで〜で間に合わせる（定型句）。
make up withは仲直りする。
make outは判別する。
make off withは持ち逃げする。
items.translation: 新しいユニフォームを買う余裕がなく、補修したジャージで間に合わせました。

items.prompt: Stretch your calves after jogging; (     ), your legs may feel stiff tomorrow.
items.explanation: ジョギング後はふくらはぎを伸ばしなさい、「さもないと（そうしないと）」明日脚がこわばるかもしれないotherwise。
distractorReasons: meanwhileはその間に。
moreoverはさらに。
otherwiseで「そうしないと」。
likewiseは同様に。
items.translation: ジョギングのあとはふくらはぎを伸ばしなさい。そうしないと明日脚が張ってしまうかもしれません。

items.prompt: The antique globe is believed to (     ) been crafted in Venice around 1750.
items.explanation: be believed to have＋過去分詞で、過去の事柄（「1750年ごろヴェネツィアで作られた」と現在信じられている）を表す完了不定詞。
distractorReasons: to havingはここでは不定詞のため不可。
toの後ろにhasは不可。
to hadは不可。
toの後ろなので原形have＋been crafted。
items.translation: その古い地球儀は1750年ごろヴェネツィアで作られたものだと考えられています。

items.prompt: No sooner had we spread our picnic mat (     ) big raindrops began to fall.
items.explanation: No sooner had S + 過去分詞 ... than ~ で「〜するやいなや…した」。シートを広げるやいなや大粒の雨が降り始めた。
distractorReasons: whenはhardly/scarcelyと組む。
no sooner ... than ~ の相関構文（比較級soonerにthanが対応）。
asは使わない。
thatは使わない。
items.translation: ピクニックシートを広げるやいなや、大粒の雨が降り始めました。

items.prompt: The tailor measured Toma's shoulders accurately and altered the jacket to (     ) him.
items.explanation: 体格や寸法が「ぴったり合う」ようにジャケットを直したfit him。
distractorReasons: fillは満たす。
fixは修理する（彼を修理するになってしまう）。
fit＋人で「（人の体にサイズが）合う」。measured shouldersと一致。
findは見つける。
items.translation: 仕立て屋はトウマの肩幅を正確に測り、彼の体にぴったり合うようジャケットを直しました。

items.prompt: Rarely (     ) wild fireflies appear beside rivers polluted with detergent.
items.explanation: 否定副詞Rarelyが文頭に出た倒置構文で、複数主語wild fireflies＋一般動詞原形appearに対応するdo。
distractorReasons: areの後ろに原形appearは不可。
Rarely do＋複数主語＋原形動詞の倒置。
haveなら過去分詞appearedが必要。

passage.title: Why Ambulance Sirens Change Pitch as They Pass
passage.text:
Stand on a sidewalk as an ambulance or express train rushes past, and you hear a familiar sound pattern: the siren sounds noticeably higher-pitched while approaching you, then drops sharply in pitch the instant the vehicle passes and speeds away. The siren speaker on the roof hasn't changed its note at all—the driver inside hears the exact same tone the whole time. Physicists call this everyday shift the "Doppler effect."

Sound travels through air as invisible waves of compressed molecules, much like ripples spreading across a pond. While an ambulance sits parked at a red light, siren waves spread outward in evenly spaced circles in every direction. Once the vehicle races forward at sixty kilometers per hour, however, it chases after its own front sound waves, squeezing consecutive wave crests closer together ahead of the bumper and stretching them farther apart behind the rear doors. Because our ears perceive closer-spaced waves as a higher musical note, bystanders ahead (21).

Astronomers and meteorologists put this exact principle to work far beyond city streets. Weather radar bounces radio waves off moving raindrops to measure wind speeds inside typhoons, while shifting starlight tells astrophysicists whether distant galaxies are (22).
passage.translation: 歩道に立っているときに救急車や急行列車が目の前を走り抜けると、近づいてくるときはサイレンの音が高く聞こえ、通り過ぎて遠ざかる瞬間にガクンと音が低くなるおなじみの現象を体験します。屋根のスピーカー自体が音程を変えているわけではなく、中に乗っている運転手にはずっと同じ高さに聞こえています。物理学者が「ドップラー効果」と呼ぶ現象です。音は空気の波として伝わりますが、車両が時速60キロで前進すると自分の出した前方の音波を追いかける形になり、進行方向では波と波の間隔が押し縮められ、後方では引き伸ばされます。人間の耳は波の間隔が狭いほど高い音として感じ取るため、前方にいる歩行者は(21)のです。天文学者や気象学者もこの原理を応用しており、気象レーダーは雨粒からの反射波で台風内部の風速を測り、星の光の波長変化からは遠い銀河が(22)かどうかを知ることができます。

passage.title: How Botanical Gardens Use Wood Libraries
passage.text:
When visitors stroll through a botanical garden or natural history museum, pressed leaves and dried blossoms in herbarium cabinets usually come to mind as plant collections. Tucked away in climate-controlled basements from Kew Gardens in London to Kyoto and Madison, Wisconsin, however, researchers curate a lesser-known archive that looks like a carpenter's dream bookshelf: thousands of polished rectangular blocks of wood shelved spine-out like hardcover novels, known as a "xylarium."

Carved from documented trees collected around the globe over the past two centuries, each block records a species' unique cellular architecture. Slice a sliver of wood thinner than tissue paper and place it under a microscope, and its water-conducting vessels, rays, and growth rings form a fingerprint as distinctive as human DNA—even decades after a tree was felled and turned into furniture or flooring.

That anatomical library now plays a frontline role against illegal logging, one of the world's most destructive wildlife crimes. Rare tropical rosewoods, mahoganies, and ebonies protected by international treaties look nearly identical to legal plantation timber once sawn into smooth planks and stacked inside shipping containers. Customs officers at ports used to rely on paper export certificates that smugglers easily forged.

By training portable machine-vision cameras and chemical spectrometers on verified xylarium blocks, wood anatomists have given border inspectors field tools that identify protected tree species on the dock within minutes.

Old museum blocks have helped art historians and luthiers too—dating medieval oak panels and matching repair wood for historic bridges—proving that carefully cataloged specimens gain unexpected value long after they are collected.
passage.translation: 植物園や自然史博物館の標本といえば押し葉標本が思い浮かびますが、ロンドンのキュー王立植物園から京都、米国ウィスコンシン州マディソンに至るまで、空調管理された収蔵庫にはハードカバーの本のように磨かれた木の直方体ブロックを何千点も並べた「木材標本館（キシラリウム）」と呼ばれる知られざる書庫があります。過去2世紀に世界各地の記録確かな樹木から切り出された木片を薄く削って顕微鏡でのぞくと、導管や放射組織、年輪の配列が樹種ごとに人間のDNAさながらの固有の指紋を示します。この解剖学的ライブラリーはいま「違法伐採」を取り締まる最前線で活躍しています。国際条約で保護される希少なローズウッドやマホガニー、黒檀も、製材されてコンテナに積まれると合法な植林材と外見ではほぼ見分けがつかず、かつて税関は偽造されやすい紙の輸出証明書に頼るしかありませんでした。しかし本物の標本ブロックを学習させた携帯型画像認識カメラや分光器のおかげで、今や港の検査官が数分で保護樹種を判別できるようになりました。中世絵画のオーク板の年代測定や歴史的木橋の補修材選定にも役立っており、丁寧に記録された標本は採取から長い時を経て思わぬ価値を発揮しています。

passage.translation: 植物園や自然史博物館の標本といえば押し葉標本が思い浮かびますが、ロンドンのキュー王立植物園から京都、米国ウィスコンシン州マディソンに至るまで、空調管理された収蔵庫にはハードカバーの本のように磨かれた木の直方体ブロックを何千点も並べた「木材標本館（キシラリウム）」と呼ばれる知られざる書庫があります。過去2世紀に世界各地の記録確かな樹木から切り出された木片を薄く削って顕微鏡でのぞくと、導管や放射組織、年輪の配列が樹種ごとに人間のDNAさながらの固有の指紋を示します。この解剖学的ライブラリーはいま「違法伐採」を取り締まる最前線で活躍しています。国際条約で保護される希少なローズウッドやマホガニー、黒檀も、製材されてコンテナに積まれると合法な植林材と外見ではほぼ見分けがつかず、かつて税関は偽造されやすい紙の輸出証明書に頼るしかありませんでした。しかし本物の標本ブロックを学習させた携帯型画像認識カメラや分光器のおかげで、今や港の検査官が数分で保護樹種を判別できるようになりました。中世絵画のオーク板の年代測定や歴史的木橋の補修材選定にも役立っており、丁寧に記録された標本は採取から長い時を経て思わぬ価値を発揮しています。

items.prompt: Why did port customs officers previously struggle to catch illegally logged rare timber?
choices: Shipping containers were transparent and never entered ports.
Sawn planks of protected trees look very similar to legal timber, and paper certificates could be faked.
International treaties protected every tree species equally.
Illegal loggers shipped whole trees with roots and birds still attached.

distractorReasons: 透明コンテナではない。
第3段落の製材後の識別困難・書類偽造問題と一致。
全樹種一律保護ではない。
根や鳥ごと運ぶのではない。

passage.title: How Botanical Gardens Use Wood Libraries
passage.text:
When visitors stroll through a botanical garden or natural history museum, pressed leaves and dried blossoms in herbarium cabinets usually come to mind as plant collections. Tucked away in climate-controlled basements from Kew Gardens in London to Kyoto and Madison, Wisconsin, however, researchers curate a lesser-known archive that looks like a carpenter's dream bookshelf: thousands of polished rectangular blocks of wood shelved spine-out like hardcover novels, known as a "xylarium."

Carved from documented trees collected around the globe over the past two centuries, each block records a species' unique cellular architecture. Slice a sliver of wood thinner than tissue paper and place it under a microscope, and its water-conducting vessels, rays, and growth rings form a fingerprint as distinctive as human DNA—even decades after a tree was felled and turned into furniture or flooring.

That anatomical library now plays a frontline role against illegal logging, one of the world's most destructive wildlife crimes. Rare tropical rosewoods, mahoganies, and ebonies protected by international treaties look nearly identical to legal plantation timber once sawn into smooth planks and stacked inside shipping containers. Customs officers at ports used to rely on paper export certificates that smugglers easily forged.

By training portable machine-vision cameras and chemical spectrometers on verified xylarium blocks, wood anatomists have given border inspectors field tools that identify protected tree species on the dock within minutes.

Old museum blocks have helped art historians and luthiers too—dating medieval oak panels and matching repair wood for historic bridges—proving that carefully cataloged specimens gain unexpected value long after they are collected.

items.prompt: How have xylarium collections strengthened port inspections recently?
choices: Customs officers burn a corner of every plank to smell the smoke.
Scientists mail heavy museum bookshelves to every cargo ship.
Verified specimens were used to train portable cameras and spectrometers that identify protected wood in minutes.
Ports banned all wooden furniture worldwide.

本棚ごと船に郵送するのではない。
第4段落のAI画像認識カメラ・分光器の訓練と現場投入の説明に一致。
木製家具全面禁止ではない。
items.translation: 近年、木材標本コレクションは港での検査をどのように強化しましたか。

items.prompt: Volunteers distributed bottled water and crackers to (     ) waiting at the shelter.
items.explanation: 避難所で待っている「住民たち」に水とクラッカーを配ったresidents。
distractorReasons: monumentsは記念碑。
incidentsは出来事・事件。
ingredientsは材料。
residentsは住民・居住者。shelterと合致。
items.translation: ボランティアたちは避難所で待機している住民にペットボトルの水とクラッカーを配りました。

items.prompt: In (     ) of the chilly wind, over three hundred runners joined the charity relay.
items.explanation: in spite of ... で「…にもかかわらず」（＝despite）。冷たい風にもかかわらず300人以上のランナーが参加した。

in spite ofで〜にもかかわらず。
in front ofは〜の前に。
in terms ofは〜の点では。
items.translation: 冷たい風が吹いていたにもかかわらず、300人以上のランナーがチャリティーリレーに参加しました。

items.explanation: 6月のカビを防ぐため、クローゼットの扉をよく開けて空気の「循環・風通し」を良くするair circulation。

calculationは計算。

concentrationは集中・濃度。
items.translation: 6月にカビを防ぐには、クローゼットの扉をこまめに開けて風通しを良くしましょう。

items.explanation: break into piecesで「粉々に（いくつもの破片に）割れる」。石けんのついた手から滑って6つほどの破片に割れた。
distractorReasons: broke into ... piecesで〜個のかけらに割れた。
ontoは〜の上へ。

items.prompt: Judging (     ) the dark clouds gathering in the west, a thunderstorm is approaching.
items.explanation: judging from ... で「…から判断すると」（慣用分詞構文）。西に集まる暗雲から判断すると雷雨が近づいている。
distractorReasons: overは使わない。
withは使わない。
intoは使わない。
Judging from ... で〜から判断すると（byも可）。

give upはあきらめる。

slip my mindでうっかり忘れる（定型句）。
senseは使わない。

hollowは空洞の。
narrowは幅の狭い。
shallow reefで水面近くの浅い岩礁。struckと合致。
items.translation: 灯台の光がなかったら、その船は浅瀬の岩礁に衝突していたかもしれません。

items.explanation: 否定語句Not until ... が文頭に出たことによる主節の疑問文語順倒置で、過去形realizedに対応するdid＋主語Mom＋原形realize。

wasの後ろに原形realizeは不可。
hadなら過去分詞realizedが必要。

自然現象の霧は禁止できない。

items.prompt:

B: (     ) Plus, the cool grass felt great on tired feet!
A: True—my ankles actually feel lighter.

items.translation: A：どうして吉田コーチは練習後に5分間、芝生の上を裸足でジョギングさせたんだろう？B：足の細かなバランス筋を鍛えるためだって言っていたよ。それに、疲れた足に冷たい芝生が気持ちよかったよね！A：たしかに——なんだか足首が軽くなった気がするよ。

Grandma sent us a box of yuzu from Kochi yesterday!
Our oven is at the library.

リンゴの木にレモンはならない。

B: (     ) Meanwhile, the second floor stays dead quiet for exam study.

So casual readers can chat softly by the coffee stand.

items.prompt:

passage.title: Why Manhole Covers Are Almost Always Round
passage.text:
Walk down almost any city street in the world, and the heavy cast-iron plates covering underground sewer and utility shafts share one unmistakable shape: they are round. Meanwhile, sidewalk grates for rainwater, subway ventilation panels, and telecom curb boxes are often rectangular. That contrast is no accident of tradition—civil engineers settled on circular manhole covers for hard-headed safety and practical reasons.

Consider what happens when workers lift a fifty-kilogram rectangular lid to climb down a ladder. Turned diagonally, a rectangle is narrower across its short side than across its corner-to-corner diagonal, meaning a careless slip could send the heavy iron plate plunging edge-first onto a technician below. A circle, by contrast, has the exact same diameter at every angle; resting on a slightly narrower circular lip inside the frame, a round cover physically (21).

Round lids simplify manufacturing and street work too. Foundries can turn circular rims smoothly on a lathe, workers never have to rotate a heavy cover to match corners when putting it back, and one worker can roll a round plate on its edge like a wheel instead of straining their back. Geometry here quietly protects (22).
passage.translation: 世界中のどの街路を歩いても、下水道や地下配管の縦坑をふさぐ重い鋳鉄製のマンホールの蓋には「丸い」という共通点があります。一方、歩道の雨水ますや地下鉄の換気口には四角い蓋もよく使われています。これには土木工学上の明確な安全・実用上の理由があります。重さ50キロの四角い蓋を外して作業員がはしごを降りる場面を考えてみましょう。長方形や正方形は対角線の長さのほうが短辺より長いため、斜めに傾けると枠をすり抜けて下の作業員の上に落下する危険があります。対照的に円はどの角度で測っても直径が完全に同じであり、ひと回り狭い受け枠の上に載せる構造にすれば丸い蓋は物理的に(21)のです。さらに旋盤で精密に加工しやすく、戻すときに向きを合わせる手間もなく、車輪のように転がして運べるため腰も痛めません。単純な幾何学が(22)の両方を静かに守っているのです。

passage.title: Preparing for the Saturday Riverbank Reed Cutting
passage.text:
From: Kasumigaura Wetland Conservation Group
To: High School Volunteer Participants
Subject: Glove rules and parking change for Saturday's reed-cutting morning

Dear student volunteers,
Thank you for signing up for our annual winter reed cutting this Saturday, January 24 (9:00 a.m. – 11:30 a.m.)! Harvesting dry winter reeds lets spring sunlight warm the shallow water so reed warblers and native minnows thrive, and local craftspeople weave the bundled stalks into traditional summer blinds (sudare).

Dry reed leaves have microscopic silica edges sharp enough to slice thin cotton knit gloves. Please wear thick leather work gloves or rubber-coated gardening gloves—we have twenty extra pairs at the tent if you don't own any.

Because bridge repairs closed the North Lot, all school vans must drop students off at the South Boat Ramp instead.

Coordinator, Wetland Group
passage.translation: 霞ヶ浦湿地保全会から高校生ボランティア参加者へのメール。今週土曜1月24日（午前9時〜11時30分）の冬のヨシ刈りへの参加感謝。枯れた冬のヨシを刈り取ることで春の日差しが浅瀬に届いてヨシキリや在来小魚が育ちやすくなり、刈り取った茎束は地元の職人が伝統的な夏のすだれに編み上げる。乾いたヨシの葉には薄い綿の軍手を切り裂くほど鋭い微細なケイ酸の縁があるため、厚手の革手袋またはゴム張り園芸手袋を着用すること（持っていない人向けにテントに予備20双あり）。橋の補修で北駐車場が閉鎖中のため、学校の送迎バンはすべて南ボートスロープで乗降すること。

items.prompt: Why shouldn't participants wear thin cotton knit gloves while cutting reeds?

Cotton gloves melt when exposed to January sunlight.

Volunteers work with bare hands in cold water.
items.explanation: Dry reed leaves have microscopic silica edges sharp enough to slice thin cotton knit gloves.とある。

1月の日光で溶けるからではない。
乾いたヨシの葉の縁が鋭く、薄い綿軍手だと切れてしまうため。
素手作業ではない。
items.translation: ヨシ刈りの際に薄い綿の軍手を使うべきでないのはなぜですか。

passage.title: How Hospital Gardens Speed Patient Recovery
passage.text:
Throughout much of the mid-twentieth century, modern hospital architecture prioritized sterile efficiency above all else. Landscaped courtyards that once surrounded nineteenth-century infirmaries were paved over for parking decks and diagnostic wings, leaving patient rooms facing blank brick walls or air-conditioning shafts.

A turning point arrived in 1984 when environmental psychologist Roger Ulrich examined ten years of surgical recovery charts at a suburban Pennsylvania hospital. Patients recovering from identical gallbladder operations had been assigned randomly to rooms along one corridor: half looked out on a small stand of deciduous trees, while the other half faced a plain brown brick wall. Patients with the tree view requested significantly fewer strong painkillers, reported lower anxiety to nurses, and went home nearly a full day sooner on average.

Follow-up clinical studies in Japan, Sweden, and the United States confirmed that visual and physical contact with greenery lowers stress hormones such as cortisol and steadies heart rate—not only in patients, but also among exhausted ICU nurses and family caregivers taking ten-minute breaks.

Today, architects design "healing gardens" onto hospital rooftops and inner courtyards with careful medical input. Smooth, glare-free paths accommodate wheelchairs and IV poles safely; fragrant herbs and seasonal blossoms help stroke patients rebuild sensory orientation, while toxic or heavy-pollen plants are excluded near allergy wards.

Greenery cannot replace skilled surgeons or antibiotics, of course, yet restoring nature to hospital grounds treats the human nervous system alongside the illness.
passage.translation: 20世紀半ばの近代病院建築は何よりも無菌的な効率性を優先し、かつて療養院を囲んでいた中庭は立体駐車場や検査棟に姿を変え、病室の窓の前には無機質なレンガ壁や空調ダクトが並ぶようになりました。転機となったのは1984年、環境心理学者のロジャー・ウルリッヒがペンシルベニア州の病院で10年分の胆嚢手術後の回復カルテを調べた研究です。同じ廊下で無作為に割り振られた病室のうち、落葉樹の木立が見える部屋の患者は茶色いレンガ壁に面した患者に比べ、強い鎮痛剤の要請が有意に少なく、不安も低く、平均で丸1日近く早く退院していたのです。その後の日本やスウェーデン、米国での臨床研究でも、緑に触れることが患者だけでなく疲弊したICU看護師や付き添い家族のストレスホルモン（コルチゾール）や心拍数を落ち着かせることが裏づけられました。今日では車椅子や点滴スタンドでも安全に通れる無反射の園路や感覚リハビリを助ける香草を備えつつ、アレルギー病棟近くでは花粉の多い植物を避けるなど、医学的知見を取り入れた屋上・中庭の「ヒーリングガーデン」が設計されています。緑が外科医や抗菌薬の代わりになるわけではありませんが、病院に自然を取り戻すことは病気と同時に人間の神経系をも癒やしてくれるのです。

items.prompt: What recovery outcomes were observed in patients whose rooms looked out onto trees?
choices: They needed fewer strong painkillers and were discharged nearly a day earlier on average.
They stayed in the hospital twice as long to watch birds.
They required three times more antibiotics.

items.explanation: requested significantly fewer strong painkillers, reported lower anxiety to nurses, and went home nearly a full day sooner on averageとある。

入院2倍長期化とは逆。

1時間で傷跡消失ではない。
items.translation: 木々が見える病室に入った患者にはどのような回復上の結果が見られましたか。

passage.title: How Hospital Gardens Speed Patient Recovery
passage.text:
Throughout much of the mid-twentieth century, modern hospital architecture prioritized sterile efficiency above all else. Landscaped courtyards that once surrounded nineteenth-century infirmaries were paved over for parking decks and diagnostic wings, leaving patient rooms facing blank brick walls or air-conditioning shafts.

A turning point arrived in 1984 when environmental psychologist Roger Ulrich examined ten years of surgical recovery charts at a suburban Pennsylvania hospital. Patients recovering from identical gallbladder operations had been assigned randomly to rooms along one corridor: half looked out on a small stand of deciduous trees, while the other half faced a plain brown brick wall. Patients with the tree view requested significantly fewer strong painkillers, reported lower anxiety to nurses, and went home nearly a full day sooner on average.

Follow-up clinical studies in Japan, Sweden, and the United States confirmed that visual and physical contact with greenery lowers stress hormones such as cortisol and steadies heart rate—not only in patients, but also among exhausted ICU nurses and family caregivers taking ten-minute breaks.

Today, architects design "healing gardens" onto hospital rooftops and inner courtyards with careful medical input. Smooth, glare-free paths accommodate wheelchairs and IV poles safely; fragrant herbs and seasonal blossoms help stroke patients rebuild sensory orientation, while toxic or heavy-pollen plants are excluded near allergy wards.

Greenery cannot replace skilled surgeons or antibiotics, of course, yet restoring nature to hospital grounds treats the human nervous system alongside the illness.
passage.translation: 20世紀半ばの近代病院建築は何よりも無菌的な効率性を優先し、かつて療養院を囲んでいた中庭は立体駐車場や検査棟に姿を変え、病室の窓の前には無機質なレンガ壁や空調ダクトが並ぶようになりました。転機となったのは1984年、環境心理学者のロジャー・ウルリッヒがペンシルベニア州の病院で10年分の胆嚢手術後の回復カルテを調べた研究です。同じ廊下で無作為に割り振られた病室のうち、落葉樹の木立が見える部屋の患者は茶色いレンガ壁に面した患者に比べ、強い鎮痛剤の要請が有意に少なく、不安も低く、平均で丸1日近く早く退院していたのです。その後の日本やスウェーデン、米国での臨床研究でも、緑に触れることが患者だけでなく疲弊したICU看護師や付き添い家族のストレスホルモン（コルチゾール）や心拍数を落ち着かせることが裏づけられました。今日では車椅子や点滴スタンドでも安全に通れる無反射の園路や感覚リハビリを助ける香草を備えつつ、アレルギー病棟近くでは花粉の多い植物を避けるなど、医学的知見を取り入れた屋上・中庭の「ヒーリングガーデン」が設計されています。緑が外科医や抗菌薬の代わりになるわけではありませんが、病院に自然を取り戻すことは病気と同時に人間の神経系をも癒やしてくれるのです。

passage.title: Borrowing More Than Books
passage.text:
A small library wanted to attract residents who rarely borrowed books. Instead of expanding its shelves, it began lending useful household objects, including a sewing machine and a set of gardening tools. The staff hoped that residents could try an object before deciding whether to buy one. People could also borrow items they needed only occasionally.

At first, the library accepted almost every donated object. This created an unexpected problem. Some items were missing parts, while others required repairs that the staff could not perform. The service soon became difficult to manage. The library therefore introduced a rule: every object had to be inspected before it was accepted. (18), donations became easier to handle, even though the library received fewer of them.

Another concern was that borrowers might return objects late. The library considered charging large fines, but staff worried this would discourage people from trying the service. Instead, borrowers received a reminder a day before an item was due. If they needed more time, they could request an extension unless someone else was waiting. The library found that clear communication was (19).

The service is still small. Staff have not claimed that it will replace shopping or solve all the town's waste problems. However, residents have started discussing which objects could usefully be shared. For the library, one important result has been (20). People who had never met now exchange advice about using and repairing the objects they borrow.
passage.translation: ある図書館は読書以外の利用者を呼び込もうと、ミシンや園芸道具など家庭用品の貸出を始めました。購入前に試したり、時々しか使わない物を借りたりできます。最初はほぼすべての寄贈品を受け入れたため、部品不足や修理不能の物が集まり、管理が難しくなりました。受入前の点検を義務化すると、(18)、数は減っても扱いやすくなりました。返却遅延には高額罰金でなく前日通知と、次の予約がない場合の延長で対応し、明確な連絡が(19)と分かりました。小規模な制度で買物の代替や廃棄物問題の全面解決は主張していませんが、共有に役立つ物について住民が話し始めました。重要な成果は(20)で、初対面の人同士が使い方や修理の助言を交換しています。

passage.title: A Sign That Needed Testing
passage.text:
Visitors to a nature reserve were often confused at a junction where two walking paths separated. One route led to a lake, while the other climbed a steep hill. To solve the problem, the reserve installed a large map. The staff were confident that a detailed map would provide all the information visitors needed.

However, volunteers noticed that many people still asked for directions. They interviewed visitors and learned that the map included many small paths but did not clearly show where the viewer was standing. The additional detail had made the map (21). The staff had thought about the whole reserve, while visitors needed to make one immediate choice.

A designer suggested placing a simple sign at the junction. It showed two arrows, the names of the destinations, and the walking time for each route. Before installing the final sign, the staff tested a temporary version for two weekends. They asked volunteers to record how often visitors stopped to ask questions. The number fell considerably. (22), fewer people accidentally began the steep route.

The detailed map was not removed. It remained useful near the entrance, where visitors could plan a longer walk. The project showed that good information is not always the largest amount of information. What matters is (23). The same person may need a broad overview at the start of a visit and a short, clear instruction at a junction.
passage.translation: 自然保護区の分岐点で来訪者が迷うため、職員は詳しい大きな地図を設置しました。しかし質問は減りません。聞き取りでは、小道は多く載っているのに現在地が不明確でした。詳細の追加が地図を(21)していたのです。職員は保護区全体、来訪者は目の前の選択を考えていました。デザイナーは矢印二つ、行き先、所要時間だけの標識を提案。仮設版を2週末試し、質問回数が大幅に減りました。(22)、誤って急な道へ進む人も減りました。詳しい地図は不要になったわけでなく、長い散策の計画を立てる入口で活用されています。情報は多ければよいのでなく、(23)ことが重要です。同じ人でも入口では全体像、分岐では簡明な指示が必要になります。

passage.title: A New Plan for the Exhibition
passage.text:
From: Elena Brooks, Project Leader
To: Student Exhibition Team
Subject: Final arrangements

Dear team,
Thank you for preparing the exhibition on the history of our neighborhood. After looking through your work, the community center has agreed to lend us its main hall. This will allow us to display larger photographs than we could in the school corridor. However, the hall is available for only one weekend, so we must finish setting up by Friday evening and remove everything on Sunday after closing.

We originally planned to borrow display boards from the town office. Unfortunately, they are needed for another event. The center has offered lightweight stands instead. These cannot hold heavy objects, so please do not bring the old tools you collected. Use photographs of them, with short explanations of what they were used for. Your interviews with residents can still be played through the small speakers.

Please send your final captions to me by Monday. I will check them for unclear dates and names, not change your choice of topics. If a resident has asked not to be named, use a description such as "a former shop owner." We have permission to show the donated photographs during the exhibition, but not to post them on social media.

I also need two volunteers to welcome visitors on Saturday morning. You do not have to know every part of local history. Your main task will be to explain the arrangement of the exhibition and direct visitors to the appropriate section. Please reply by tomorrow if you can help.

Elena

passage.title: Keeping Track of City Trees
passage.text:
On a summer afternoon, a tree-lined street can feel quite different from a nearby road without shade. Trees also provide places for birds and insects to live. Yet city officials often have incomplete information about the trees they are responsible for. Paper records may be old, and different departments may keep separate lists. This can make it difficult to decide where care is most urgently needed.

In one city, a group of residents offered to help create a shared tree record. Volunteers walked along public streets and entered basic information into a mobile form. They recorded each tree's location, took a photograph, and noted visible signs of damage. They were not asked to judge whether a tree was safe. That decision remained the responsibility of trained specialists.

The first month produced thousands of entries, but some were unreliable. A tree near a street corner might be recorded by two teams, while a photograph taken from far away might show the wrong tree. Rather than simply count the entries, the project leader introduced a checking stage. Teams compared neighboring records, and specialists reviewed reports of possible disease. Each confirmed tree received a single identification number.

The resulting map changed how the city planned its work. Officials had previously responded mainly to requests from residents. However, some neighborhoods made many requests while others made few, even when their trees were in poor condition. The new record allowed officials to compare areas more fairly. It also revealed streets where there were very few trees at all.

The project did not mean that every neighborhood could immediately receive new trees. Planting requires money, and there must be enough space underground for roots as well as above ground for branches. In some streets, water pipes and cables limited the available space. Officials had to explain why a request could not always be accepted.

For volunteers, the main lesson was that collecting information was only the beginning. The value of the record depended on checking it, keeping it current, and using it to answer practical questions. The group now revisits a different area each month. Its members hope that a record built through public participation will remain useful because people understand both its purpose and its limits.
passage.translation: 木陰のある街路は暑い午後にも涼しく感じられ、生き物の場所にもなります。しかし行政の樹木記録は古く、部署ごとに分かれ、必要な手入れの優先順位をつけにくいことがあります。ある市では住民が所在地、写真、目に見える損傷を記録しました。安全性の判断は専門家に残しました。当初は重複や別の木の写真が混じったため、近隣記録の比較と専門家の確認を追加し、確認済みの木に一意の番号を付与しました。従来は住民の要望中心で、声の多い地域と少ない地域の偏りがありましたが、新記録でより公平に比較でき、木の少ない街路も分かりました。ただし費用や根・枝の空間、地下の配管やケーブルの制約があり、すべての希望地にすぐ植樹できません。住民にはその理由の説明が必要でした。情報の収集は出発点であり、点検・更新・実際の判断への活用が価値を決めます。住民は毎月地域を変えて再確認し、目的と限界を理解する参加者がいることで記録が役立ち続けると期待しています。

passage.title: Why Supermarkets Adjust Their Music
passage.text:
Shoppers rarely pay conscious attention to the music playing overhead while they push a cart down an aisle. Yet retail researchers have long studied how tempo and volume subtly shape behavior inside stores. Fast, energetic songs tend to make people walk more briskly, whereas slower instrumental tracks encourage customers to pause and examine shelves.

A regional grocery chain recently reconsidered its daytime playlist after receiving feedback from older residents and parents of young children. Many found the combination of bright lights, announcements, and upbeat pop songs exhausting. In response, the chain introduced "quiet mornings" twice a week, turning off promotional broadcasts and lowering music volume. (18), complaints dropped and weekday morning visits grew steadily.

Interestingly, staff members benefited just as much as shoppers. Cashiers and shelf stockers spend up to eight hours in the store, hearing the same loop of songs repeatedly. When the store switched to calmer, varied acoustic pieces during regular hours, employees reported feeling less fatigued at the end of a shift. This mattered because (19).

The chain did not eliminate lively music altogether; weekend afternoon sales events still feature brighter playlists. However, managers stopped treating background sound as mere filler. They learned that (20) can make an ordinary errand noticeably less stressful for everyone inside the building.
passage.translation: 買い物客は店内の音楽を意識することはまれですが、曲の速さや音量は行動に微妙な影響を与えます。速い曲は足取りを速め、ゆっくりした器楽曲は棚をじっくり見る行動を促します。ある地域のスーパーは高齢者や子育て世帯から「明るい照明と館内放送、賑やかな曲の重なりで疲れる」との声を受け、週2回の「静かな朝」を導入して宣伝放送を止め音量を下げました。(18)、苦情は減り平日の朝の利用者が着実に増えました。さらに8時間同じ曲を聴き続けるレジ係や品出し係も、通常時間帯の曲が穏やかで多様なアコースティック曲に変わったことで勤務後の疲労軽減を実感しました。これは重要で、なぜなら(19)からです。週末午後の特売では明るい曲も残しましたが、経営陣はBGMを単なる埋め草とみなすのをやめ、(20)が誰にとっても買い物の負担を減らすと学びました。

passage.title: Saving Seeds in School Gardens
passage.text:
Many elementary and junior high schools plant cherry tomatoes or sunflowers each spring using packets of commercial seeds. Students water the beds, harvest the crop in summer, and clear the plot in autumn. The next April, teachers buy fresh seed packets and repeat the cycle. While children learn how plants grow, they seldom see how one generation of plants produces the next.

A group of science teachers in Nagano decided to extend this lesson by teaching students to collect and store seeds from their own harvest. The task turned out to require more care than simply drying a few pods on a windowsill. If seeds were sealed in jars while still slightly damp, mold ruined them over winter. Students had to measure weight changes over several days to confirm that the seeds were dry enough. (21), the project connected biology with careful data recording.

The teachers also noticed an unexpected change in how students treated the garden in late summer. Plants that had finished fruiting were once pulled up right away because they looked untidy. Once students understood that seed pods needed weeks on the stem to ripen fully, they put up small explanatory signs rather than clearing the beds prematurely. Visitors learned that the brown stalks were (22).

Not every saved seed sprouted the following spring, and cross-pollination occasionally produced surprising shapes in pumpkins. Far from being failures, these variations sparked lively classroom questions about genetics. Passing labeled envelopes of seeds to the incoming grade gave students (23).
passage.translation: 多くの小中学校では毎年春に市販の種を買ってミニトマトやヒマワリを育て、秋に片づけて翌春また新しい種を買います。植物の成長は学べても世代がつながる仕組みは見えにくいままでした。長野の理科教員グループは収穫物から種を採取・保存する授業を始めましたが、窓辺で乾かすだけでは不十分で、少しでも湿気が残ると冬にカビが生えました。数日間の重量変化を測って乾燥を確かめる必要があり、(21)、生物の観察と丁寧なデータ記録が結びつきました。晩夏の畑の扱いも変わり、以前は見た目が悪いとすぐ抜いていた枯れ茎も、種が熟すのに数週間要ると分かると説明札を立てて残すようになり、来校者にも茶色い茎が(22)と伝わりました。翌春すべてが発芽するとは限らず交雑で珍しい形のカボチャもできましたが、それが遺伝への疑問を呼び、次の学年へ種袋を引き継ぐことで生徒は(23)を得ました。

passage.title: Saving Seeds in School Gardens
passage.text:
Many elementary and junior high schools plant cherry tomatoes or sunflowers each spring using packets of commercial seeds. Students water the beds, harvest the crop in summer, and clear the plot in autumn. The next April, teachers buy fresh seed packets and repeat the cycle. While children learn how plants grow, they seldom see how one generation of plants produces the next.

A group of science teachers in Nagano decided to extend this lesson by teaching students to collect and store seeds from their own harvest. The task turned out to require more care than simply drying a few pods on a windowsill. If seeds were sealed in jars while still slightly damp, mold ruined them over winter. Students had to measure weight changes over several days to confirm that the seeds were dry enough. (21), the project connected biology with careful data recording.

The teachers also noticed an unexpected change in how students treated the garden in late summer. Plants that had finished fruiting were once pulled up right away because they looked untidy. Once students understood that seed pods needed weeks on the stem to ripen fully, they put up small explanatory signs rather than clearing the beds prematurely. passage.title: Relocating the Career Talk Sessions
passage.text:
From: Career Guidance Office
To: Second-Year High School Students
Subject: Room changes and question cards for Friday's Career Day

Dear students,
This Friday afternoon, twelve graduates working in fields ranging from nursing to civil engineering will visit our school for Career Day. Because more students signed up for the architecture and healthcare sessions than Room 201 and Room 202 can safely seat, those two sessions have been moved to the audiovisual hall and the library reading room. All other sessions remain in their original classrooms; please check the updated map posted outside the staff room.

Each guest will speak for twenty minutes and then spend fifteen minutes answering student questions. Rather than calling on hands randomly, student moderators will group similar questions together so more topics can be covered. For this reason, please submit at least one question through the class link by Wednesday at 5:00 p.m.

You will attend two sessions during the afternoon. Leave your backpacks in your homeroom and bring only a pen, your notepad, and your indoor shoes. Taking photographs or recording audio during the talks is not permitted, as several speakers will share workplace examples that are not for public distribution.

Career Guidance Office
passage.translation: 進路指導室から高校2年生への連絡。今週金曜午後のキャリアデーには看護から土木工学まで12名の卒業生が来校する。建築と医療の分科会は201・202教室の安全定員を超える申込があったため、視聴覚ホールと図書館閲覧室へ変更。他の分科会は元の教室のままなので職員室前の更新マップを確認すること。各講師は20分講演の後、15分質疑応答を行う。その場で無作為に挙手を当てるのではなく、より多くの話題を扱えるよう生徒司会者が似た質問をまとめるため、水曜午後5時までにクラスのリンクから最低1問提出すること。午後に2つの分科会へ参加する。リュックはホームルームに置き、ペン・メモ帳・上履きのみ持参。職場内の非公開事例が含まれるため写真撮影や録音は禁止。

passage.title: Repair Cafes and How Products Are Designed
passage.text:
Across many cities, weekend "repair cafes" invite residents to bring broken toasters, lamps, and bicycles to community halls where skilled volunteers help fix them for free. Most visitors come with a practical goal: extending the life of a household item and keeping it out of the trash. Over the past decade, however, these grassroots gatherings have begun producing something else of value—detailed records of why everyday appliances fail.

Volunteers at dozens of repair groups log each item's brand, approximate age, and the specific fault they encountered. When thousands of entries are combined, clear patterns emerge. For example, a handheld vacuum might have a motor capable of running for ten years, yet be discarded after two because a tiny plastic latch on the dust cup snaps and no spare part is sold. Similarly, some kettles cannot be opened without breaking glued seams, making even a simple switch repair nearly impossible.

Consumer advocacy groups and engineering schools have started using this shared data in constructive ways. Design instructors assign students to examine broken appliances from repair logs and redesign weak joints or sealed casings so they can be unscrewed with standard household tools. Meanwhile, policy discussions in several countries now reference repair-cafe statistics when proposing rules that require manufacturers to supply basic replacement parts for a set number of years.

Manufacturers sometimes argue that sealed, lightweight designs keep production costs low and protect users from tampering with dangerous electrical components. Safety is a legitimate concern, especially with high-voltage devices. For that reason, repair advocates distinguish between parts that ordinary owners can safely swap—such as filters, batteries, and latches—and internal components that should only be serviced by certified technicians.

Ultimately, the data gathered at neighborhood tables shows that durability is shaped long before an item breaks. While volunteers can rescue individual machines one Saturday at a time, lasting waste reduction depends on feeding those hands-on lessons back into how products are engineered in the first place.
passage.translation: 多くの都市で週末に開かれる「リペアカフェ」では、壊れたトースターや照明、自転車を住民が持ち込み、技術を持つボランティアと無料で修理します。当初の目的は日用品の寿命を延ばしごみを減らすことでしたが、ここ10年で「家電がなぜ壊れるのか」という詳細な記録を生み出す場にもなっています。各地の団体が製品の種類・使用年数・故障箇所を記録して何千件も集約すると明確な傾向が見えてきます。例えばモーターは10年動くのにダストカップの小さなプラスチック留め具が2年で折れ交換部品も売られていない掃除機や、接着されていて開けると壊れるためスイッチひとつ直せない電気ケトルなどです。消費者団体や工学系の学校はこのデータを活用し、標準工具で分解できる設計演習や、一定期間の交換部品供給を義務づける政策議論に役立てています。メーカー側は密閉軽量設計の低コスト性や高電圧部への安全性を挙げますが、推進派も一般利用者が安全に交換できる部品と有資格技術者が扱う内部部品を区別しています。地域の修理台から集まった知見を最初の製品設計へ還元することが、持続的な廃棄物削減のカギを握っています。

To explain why volunteers refuse to touch cleaning devices.

小さな部品の破損と部品未供給で製品全体が廃棄される例。
モーターは10年動くとある。
ボランティアが拒否したとはない。
items.translation: 著者が第2段落でハンディ掃除機に言及しているのはなぜですか。
