passage.title: How District Cooling Chills Buildings from Underground Pipes
passage.text:
Walk past a row of glass office towers on a sweltering August afternoon, and you might expect every rooftop to roar with its own bank of air-conditioning condensers. In dense districts of cities such as Sapporo, Stockholm, Toronto, and Singapore, however, many large buildings contain no individual chillers at all. Instead, they draw icy water from a shared underground loop operated by a central "district cooling" plant.

Pooling cooling demand across dozens of offices, hospitals, and shopping arcades unlocks efficiencies that single buildings cannot match. Offices peak at two in the afternoon while hotels need more cooling at night, allowing one central plant to run steady, high-efficiency turbines rather than starting and stopping dozens of small motors. Central plants can also tap natural cold sources unavailable to individual rooftops—such as deep lake water, seawater, or winter snow stored in insulated pits until July. (21), electricity demand during summer heat waves drops sharply.

Urban neighborhoods feel the difference outdoors too. Individual rooftop units pump hot exhaust air straight into narrow streets, worsening the urban heat-island effect right where pedestrians walk. Moving heat rejection to a single waterfront facility keeps downtown air noticeably cooler and quieter. (22), freeing up rooftop space allows architects to install solar panels or shaded sky gardens.

Digging insulated pipe networks beneath existing streets requires heavy upfront investment, so district cooling works best in compact areas. Even so, shared thermal networks offer cities (23).
passage.translation: うだるような8月の午後、ガラス張りのオフィスビル街を歩けばどの屋上でも大型エアコンの室外機がうなりを上げていると思いがちです。しかし札幌、ストックホルム、トロント、シンガポールなどの高密度地区では、個別の冷却機を一切持たず、中央の「地域冷房」プラントから地下配管ループで冷水を受け取っている大型ビルが少なくありません。何十棟ものオフィス、病院、商業施設の冷房需要を束ねることで単独ビルでは不可能な効率が生まれます。オフィスは午後2時にピークを迎える一方ホテルは夜間に需要が増えるため、小型モーターを何十台も発停させる代わりに高効率の大型タービンを安定稼働させられ、深層の湖水や海水、7月まで断熱槽に蓄えた冬の雪といった自然冷熱も活用できます。(21)、夏の猛暑時の電力需要が大幅に下がります。屋外の街並みにも恩恵があり、屋上室外機が狭い通りに熱風を吐き出してヒートアイランド現象を悪化させるのを防ぎ、街なかをより涼しく静かに保てます。(22)、空いた屋上スペースに太陽光パネルや緑豊かな屋上庭園を設けることもできます。既存道路の下に断熱配管を埋設する初期投資は大きいため高密度地区向きですが、共有熱ネットワークは都市に(23)をもたらします。

passage.title: How District Cooling Chills Buildings from Underground Pipes
passage.text:
Walk past a row of glass office towers on a sweltering August afternoon, and you might expect every rooftop to roar with its own bank of air-conditioning condensers. In dense districts of cities such as Sapporo, Stockholm, Toronto, and Singapore, however, many large buildings contain no individual chillers at all. Instead, they draw icy water from a shared underground loop operated by a central "district cooling" plant.

Pooling cooling demand across dozens of offices, hospitals, and shopping arcades unlocks efficiencies that single buildings cannot match. Offices peak at two in the afternoon while hotels need more cooling at night, allowing one central plant to run steady, high-efficiency turbines rather than starting and stopping dozens of small motors. Central plants can also tap natural cold sources unavailable to individual rooftops—such as deep lake water, seawater, or winter snow stored in insulated pits until July. (21), electricity demand during summer heat waves drops sharply.

Urban neighborhoods feel the difference outdoors too. Individual rooftop units pump hot exhaust air straight into narrow streets, worsening the urban heat-island effect right where pedestrians walk. Moving heat rejection to a single waterfront facility keeps downtown air noticeably cooler and quieter. (22), freeing up rooftop space allows architects to install solar panels or shaded sky gardens.

Digging insulated pipe networks beneath existing streets requires heavy upfront investment, so district cooling works best in compact areas. Even so, shared thermal networks offer cities (23).

passage.title: Updated Policy for Borrowing Field Recording Kits
passage.text:
From: Media Lab Desk, Faculty of Cultural Studies
To: Undergraduate Fieldwork Students
Subject: Windscreens and memory-card rules for oral-history kits

Dear students,
Starting next Monday, six upgraded stereo audio kits will be available for two-week loan to students conducting local oral-history interviews this semester. Before reserving a kit online, please note two updated borrowing rules based on issues from last autumn.

First, every kit now includes a furry "deadcat" wind muff alongside the standard foam sponge cover. Foam covers stop indoor breath pops, but they cannot block wind rumble on porches, farms, or fishing piers; three outdoor interviews last term were almost impossible to transcribe because of wind noise. Whenever you record outdoors, slip the furry wind muff over the microphone before pressing record.

Second, the Media Lab no longer lends SD memory cards inside the cases. Last year, two students accidentally returned kits before copying their files, and our automatic formatting bench erased a week's worth of recordings. Please purchase your own Class-10 SD card (32 GB or 64 GB) at the campus co-op and test it in the recorder at the pickup counter before leaving.

Happy interviewing,
Media Lab Staff
passage.translation: 文化学部メディアラボ窓口からフィールドワーク履修学生への連絡。来週月曜より、今学期の地域オーラルヒストリー調査向けに新型ステレオ録音キット6台を2週間貸し出す。昨秋のトラブルを踏まえた2つの改定ルールを確認すること。第1に、通常のスポンジ風防に加えて毛足の長い防風マフを同梱した。スポンジは室内の息の音は防げるが縁側や畑、漁港での風切り音は防げず、前学期は屋外録音3件が文字起こし困難になったため、屋外録音時は必ず毛の防風マフを装着すること。第2に、ケース内でのSDカード貸出を廃止した。昨年、データをコピーし忘れたまま返却されたカードが自動初期化機で消去される事故が2件起きたため、生協で各自のSDカードを購入し、貸出窓口で本体に入れて動作確認してから持ち出すこと。

passage.title: Why Bookbinders Still Sew Heavy-Use Books with Thread
passage.text:
Pick up an inexpensive paperback novel, and you will see its pages held together by a thin layer of flexible glue along a flat spine. Invented to speed up mass publishing in the twentieth century, adhesive "perfect binding" made books affordable for millions of readers and works admirably for novels read once or twice on a train. Ask a chef, pianist, or reference librarian which binding they trust, however, and many will immediately point to sewn signatures.

In traditional Smyth-sewn binding, large printed sheets are folded into small booklets of sixteen or thirty-two pages—called signatures—and stitched through the fold with strong cotton or linen thread before all the booklets are linked together. The practical difference appears the moment you set the book on a table. Because glued paperbacks rely on stiff spine adhesive to grip individual cut edges, pressing a paperback flat on a kitchen counter or piano music desk often cracks the spine and sends loose pages fluttering to the floor. A sewn book, by contrast, flexes along its folded hinges and lies wide open hands-free without straining the binding.

Longevity matters just as much for archives and schools. Even high-grade synthetic glues gradually oxidize and turn brittle over decades, especially in dry heated rooms or humid tropical libraries. Linen thread stitched through acid-free paper routinely endures for centuries; when a sewn library dictionary eventually wears out its cloth cover, a conservator can replace the outer case while leaving the intact text block untouched.

Modern automated sewing machines have narrowed the cost gap, allowing textbook publishers and art museums to order sewn runs without handcraft delays. Glued paperbacks will always dominate airport bookstalls, yet wherever a book must stay open on a workbench or serve generations of readers, needle and thread remain unmatched.
passage.translation: 安価なペーパーバック小説を手に取ると、平らな背に沿った薄い接着剤の層でページが留められているのが分かります。20世紀の大量出版を加速させた「無線綴じ」は本を手頃な価格にし、電車で1〜2度読む小説には十分機能します。しかし料理人やピアニスト、レファレンス司書に信頼する製本方式を尋ねれば、多くが迷わず「糸かがり綴じ」を挙げます。伝統的なスマイス式糸かがり製本では、大きな印刷紙を16ページや32ページの「折丁」に折り、折り目を丈夫な綿糸や麻糸で縫ってから束ねます。違いは机に置いた瞬間に現れます。切り落とした紙の断面を硬い接着剤で固定する無線綴じは、調理台やピアノの譜面台に平らに押し開くと背が割れてページが抜け落ちがちですが、糸かがり本は折り目を蝶番にして手放しでも無理なく開いたまま保てます。公文書館や学校にとっては耐久性も重要で、合成接着剤が数十年で酸化してもろくなるのに対し、中性紙を麻糸で縫った本は何世紀も持ち、表紙が傷んでも中身をそのままに外装だけ張り替えられます。自動糸かがり機の進歩でコスト差も縮まっており、作業台で開きっぱなしにする本や世代を超えて使う本では今も針と糸が最良の選択であり続けています。

passage.title: Why Bookbinders Still Sew Heavy-Use Books with Thread
passage.text:
Pick up an inexpensive paperback novel, and you will see its pages held together by a thin layer of flexible glue along a flat spine. Invented to speed up mass publishing in the twentieth century, adhesive "perfect binding" made books affordable for millions of readers and works admirably for novels read once or twice on a train. Ask a chef, pianist, or reference librarian which binding they trust, however, and many will immediately point to sewn signatures.

In traditional Smyth-sewn binding, large printed sheets are folded into small booklets of sixteen or thirty-two pages—called signatures—and stitched through the fold with strong cotton or linen thread before all the booklets are linked together. The practical difference appears the moment you set the book on a table. Because glued paperbacks rely on stiff spine adhesive to grip individual cut edges, pressing a paperback flat on a kitchen counter or piano music desk often cracks the spine and sends loose pages fluttering to the floor. A sewn book, by contrast, flexes along its folded hinges and lies wide open hands-free without straining the binding.

Longevity matters just as much for archives and schools. Even high-grade synthetic glues gradually oxidize and turn brittle over decades, especially in dry heated rooms or humid tropical libraries. Linen thread stitched through acid-free paper routinely endures for centuries; when a sewn library dictionary eventually wears out its cloth cover, a conservator can replace the outer case while leaving the intact text block untouched.

Modern automated sewing machines have narrowed the cost gap, allowing textbook publishers and art museums to order sewn runs without handcraft delays. Glued paperbacks will always dominate airport bookstalls, yet wherever a book must stay open on a workbench or serve generations of readers, needle and thread remain unmatched.

passage.title: Why Supermarkets Place Bakeries and Flowers Near the Entrance
passage.text:
Step through the automatic doors of many large supermarkets, and instead of canned soup or laundry detergent, you are greeted by buckets of seasonal flowers and the warm scent of baking bread. Retail planners rarely leave store layouts to chance, and dedicating prime entrance floor space to fragile petals and ovens reflects decades of consumer psychology research.

Shoppers arriving from busy streets or parking lots carry mental haste; people walking briskly tend to grab only the three items on their list and head straight for the register. Bright colors and the aroma of fresh crust trigger sensory associations with freshness and home cooking, prompting visitors to slow their pace and browse more attentively. (18), customers judge the quality of the entire store—including packaged goods aisles farther back—more favorably when their first impression feels vibrant and farm-fresh.

Practical handling plays a role in flower placement, though bread and produce require careful cart choreography too. Soft berries and bouquets get crushed if piled beneath milk cartons and canned tomatoes at the end of a trip. Placing delicate items in the upper child-seat basket right at the start keeps them safe, or reminds shoppers to pick up a bouquet on their way out. (19), checkout lanes are stocked with small impulse treats at eye level while people wait.

Understanding store geography helps everyday consumers enjoy pleasant displays while (20).
passage.translation: 多くの大型スーパーマーケットの自動ドアをくぐると、缶詰や洗濯洗剤ではなく、季節の花々と焼きたてのパンの温かい香りに出迎えられます。店舗設計者が売り場配置を偶然に任せることはめったになく、入口の一等地に傷みやすい花びらやオーブンを置く背景には何十年もの消費者心理学の研究があります。せわしない通りや駐車場から入ってくる買い物客は気持ちが急いており、早足のままではメモの3品だけを取ってレジへ直行しがちです。鮮やかな色彩と焼きたてのパンの香りは新鮮さや家庭料理への連想を呼び起こし、自然と歩調を緩めて店内をじっくり見て回る気持ちにさせます。(18)、最初の印象が生き生きとして新鮮だと、奥の加工食品売り場を含む店全体の品質までも好意的に評価する傾向があります。また柔らかいベリー類や花束は買い物の最後に牛乳パックやトマト缶の下敷きになると潰れてしまうため、カートの子ども席かごの分かりやすい位置へ最初に載せるか帰りに買う意識づけにもなり、(19)、レジ待ちの列では目線の高さに小さな菓子類が並べられます。売り場の配置意図を知っておけば、心地よい陳列を楽しみつつ(20)ことができます。

passage.title: Why Supermarkets Place Bakeries and Flowers Near the Entrance
passage.text:
Step through the automatic doors of many large supermarkets, and instead of canned soup or laundry detergent, you are greeted by buckets of seasonal flowers and the warm scent of baking bread. Retail planners rarely leave store layouts to chance, and dedicating prime entrance floor space to fragile petals and ovens reflects decades of consumer psychology research.

Shoppers arriving from busy streets or parking lots carry mental haste; people walking briskly tend to grab only the three items on their list and head straight for the register. Bright colors and the aroma of fresh crust trigger sensory associations with freshness and home cooking, prompting visitors to slow their pace and browse more attentively. (18), customers judge the quality of the entire store—including packaged goods aisles farther back—more favorably when their first impression feels vibrant and farm-fresh.

Practical handling plays a role in flower placement, though bread and produce require careful cart choreography too. Soft berries and bouquets get crushed if piled beneath milk cartons and canned tomatoes at the end of a trip. Placing delicate items in the upper child-seat basket right at the start keeps them safe, or reminds shoppers to pick up a bouquet on their way out. (19), checkout lanes are stocked with small impulse treats at eye level while people wait.

Understanding store geography helps everyday consumers enjoy pleasant displays while (20).

passage.title: How Salt Marshes Protect Coasts and Store Carbon
passage.text:
For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, tidal salt marshes—low coastal grasslands flooded twice daily by seawater—were dismissed by planners as muddy wasteland. Across Europe, East Asia, and North America, thousands of hectares were drained behind dikes to create pasture, factory sites, or port landfills.

Only after costly storm surges battered reclaimed shorelines did engineers measure what had been lost. Dense mats of salt-tolerant cordgrass and rushes act like a giant natural sponge and brake: friction from millions of flexible stems slows incoming storm waves and lowers flood peaks before water reaches inland homes. Unlike rigid concrete walls, healthy marshes trap river sediment on every tide, allowing the ground surface to build upward gradually over decades. (21), coastal towns behind wide marshes often spend far less on seawall repairs.

Climate researchers uncovered a second superpower hidden in the mud below. On land, fallen forest leaves decompose in oxygen-rich soil and release most of their carbon back into the air within years. Waterlogged marsh mud contains almost no oxygen, however, slowing microbial decay to a crawl. Dead marsh roots accumulate in thick peat layers meters deep, locking carbon away for centuries—a process scientists call "blue carbon." (22), restoring breached dikes to let tides return revives nursery habitats for young flounder and crabs.

Protecting surviving tidal marshes is therefore no luxury; it represents (23).
passage.translation: 19世紀から20世紀の長い間、1日に2度海水に浸かる沿岸の塩性湿地は、都市計画者から泥だらけの荒れ地と見なされてきました。欧州、東アジア、北米の各地で何千ヘクタールもの湿地が堤防で干拓され、牧草地や工場用地、港湾埋立地に変えられました。しかし埋め立てた海岸線が高潮で大きな被害を受けて初めて、技術者たちは失われた機能を数値で知ることになりました。塩分に強いアシやイグサが密生する群落は巨大なスポンジ兼ブレーキとして働き、幾百万ものしなやかな茎の摩擦が高波を減速させ内陸の住宅に届く前に浸水ピークを下げます。硬いコンクリート壁と違い、健全な湿地は潮の満ち引きごとに土砂を捉えて数十年かけ地面を少しずつ高くしていきます。(21)、広い湿地に守られた沿岸の町では護岸の修繕費が大幅に抑えられることが少なくありません。さらに気候研究者は泥の中に眠る第2の力も発見しました。陸の森の落ち葉は酸素の多い土壌で数年以内に分解され炭素を大気へ戻しますが、水に浸かった湿地の泥には酸素がほとんどないため微生物分解が極端に遅く、枯れた根が何メートルもの泥炭層となって何世紀も炭素を閉じ込める「ブルーカーボン」として機能します。(22)、古い堤防を開いて潮を戻せばヒラメやカニの稚魚のゆりかごも蘇ります。残された干潟や塩性湿地を守ることは贅沢ではなく、(23)なのです。

passage.title: Notice Regarding Shared Bicycle Permits on Campus
passage.text:
From: Campus Traffic & Safety Office
To: All Commuting Students
Subject: New reflector inspection and abandoned-bike tags starting May 1

Dear commuting students,
With more than 1,400 bicycles using the North and West campus racks daily, rack shortages and evening near-misses at the main slope have increased this spring. Starting May 1, the Campus Traffic Office is updating registration rules for all 2026–2027 bicycle permits.

To receive your blue 2026 sticker, bring your bicycle in person to the East Gate booth between April 20 and April 30 (12:10 p.m. – 1:00 p.m. or 4:15 p.m. – 5:30 p.m.). Staff will check three items before issuing a sticker: working front headlights, a rear red reflector or tail lamp, and an audible bell. Online applications alone will no longer be accepted, as many registered bikes lacked working lights last winter.

In addition, bicycles parked without a valid 2026 sticker—or left unmoved in the same rack space for over thirty days—will receive a yellow warning tag on May 11. Tagged bicycles not claimed within fourteen days will be moved to the South Storage Lot.

Thank you for helping keep campus paths safe,
Campus Traffic & Safety Office
passage.translation: 大学構内交通・安全室から自転車通学の学生全員へのメール。北・西駐輪場を毎日1400台以上の自転車が利用する中、今春はラック不足と正面坂道での夕方のヒヤリハットが増えているため、5月1日より駐輪許可証ルールを改定する。青い2026年ステッカーを受け取るには、4月20日〜30日に東門ブースへ実車を持ち込むこと。昨冬は無灯火の登録車が多かったためオンライン申請のみは廃止し、前照灯・後部赤色反射板（または尾灯）・ベルの3点をスタッフが確認したうえで交付する。また有効なステッカーのない自転車や同じ区画に30日以上放置された自転車には5月11日に黄色い警告札を付け、14日以内に引き取りがない場合は南保管所へ移動する。

passage.title: Why Pianists Watch Humidity More Than Temperature
passage.text:
Walk backstage at a symphony hall, and you may spot a small digital hygrometer sitting right beside the grand piano. Audience members naturally notice whether a hall feels warm or chilly, yet piano technicians worry far more about relative humidity—the percentage of moisture held in the air. Keeping an acoustic piano in tune and responsive depends above all on protecting its wooden heart: the soundboard.

Beneath a grand piano's heavy cast-iron frame and steel strings—which pull with nearly twenty tons of combined tension—stretches a thin, slightly arched sheet of Sitka spruce called the soundboard. Strings alone move very little air; they rely on wooden bridges pressed against that arched spruce board to amplify vibrations into rich musical tone. Because wood is hygroscopic, its cells swell when indoor air is humid in summer and shrink when winter heating dries the hall.

As the soundboard swells in damp July air, its upward arch pushes harder against the strings, stretching them tighter and raising the piano's pitch noticeably—especially in the middle register. Conversely, dry January air flattens the arch slightly, letting string tension drop so notes go flat and lose warmth. Repeated swings between eighty percent summer humidity and twenty percent winter dryness can eventually split the spruce seams or loosen the thousands of wooden pins holding the strings.

Major concert venues therefore invest heavily in climate-controlled "piano garages" backstage, maintaining relative humidity close to forty-five percent year-round. Where full building humidification is impractical—such as in historic stone churches or school auditoriums—technicians mount slender climate systems directly underneath the piano belly: a low-wattage warming rod gently dries damp summer air, while a wick reservoir adds moisture in winter.

A pianist's artistry begins at the keys, yet the stability of every chord rests quietly on keeping centuries-old wood science in balance.
passage.translation: シンフォニーホールの舞台裏を歩くと、グランドピアノのすぐ横に小さなデジタル湿度計が置かれているのを見かけることがあります。観客が気にするのは室温の暑さ寒さですが、ピアノ調律師がはるかに気を配るのは空気中の水分割合である「相対湿度」であり、その中心にあるのが木製の心臓部「響板」の保護です。合計約20トンもの張力で張られた鋼鉄弦と鋳鉄フレームの下には、わずかに反りを持たせた薄いシトカスプルース材の響板が広がっており、弦の振動を豊かな音へと増幅しています。木材には吸湿性があるため、夏の湿った空気では膨張して響板のアーチが弦を押し上げ、特に中音域のピッチを高くしてしまいます。逆に冬の暖房で乾いた空気ではアーチがわずかに平らになって弦の張力が落ち、音が低く痩せてしまいます。激しい湿度変化を繰り返すと、やがて響板の継ぎ目が割れたり何千本ものチューニングピンが緩んだりしかねません。そのため一流ホールは年間を通じて湿度45％前後を保つ専用の保管庫を備え、石造教会や学校の講堂など建物全体の空調が難しい場所ではピアノ底面に小型の除湿ヒーターと加湿器を取り付ける工夫で音色と調律を守っています。

items.prompt: Why does a piano's pitch tend to rise during humid summer weather?
choices: Pianists strike the keys harder in July.
Steel strings shrink to half their length when damp.
Stage spotlights melt the tuning pins.
Moisture makes the wooden soundboard swell upward, pushing harder against the strings and increasing tension.
items.explanation: As the soundboard swells in damp July air, its upward arch pushes harder against the strings, stretching them tighter and raising the piano's pitchとある。
distractorReasons: 強く叩くからではない。
鋼鉄弦が半分の長さに縮むことはない。
ピンが溶けることはない。
第3段落前半のメカニズムと一致。
items.translation: 湿度の高い夏の時期にピアノの音程が上がりやすいのはなぜですか。

items.prompt: What long-term structural damage can extreme seasonal swings in humidity cause?
choices: Spruce soundboard seams may crack and wooden tuning pins can loosen.
The cast-iron frame turns into soft copper.
Black keys lose their color in sunlight.
items.explanation: Repeated swings ... can eventually split the spruce seams or loosen the thousands of wooden pins holding the stringsとある。
distractorReasons: 第3段落末の記述と一致。
鉄が銅に変わることはない。
黒鍵の退色ではない。

items.translation: 季節による極端な湿度変化の繰り返しは、長期的にどのような構造的損傷を引き起こし得ますか。

passage.title: Why Escalator Handrails Move Slightly Faster Than the Steps
passage.text:
Anyone who holds onto an escalator handrail during a long subway ride has probably noticed a tiny quirk: after twenty seconds, your hand has crept a couple of centimeters ahead of your body, forcing you to move your fingers back. Commuters often assume the belt is poorly calibrated. In reality, technicians adjust many escalators so the rubber handrail runs roughly one to two percent faster than the metal steps.

Mechanical wear explains part of the design. While the steps are driven by toothed steel chains that never slip, the rubber handrail is pulled over smooth rollers by friction. As rollers age, slight slippage naturally slows the belt down. Setting a new handrail marginally fast ensures it will not lag behind the steps months later. (18), safety researchers point out an important human-balance reason behind that forward bias.

Imagine standing on steep steps rising at thirty degrees if the handrail moved slower than your feet: your arm would gradually get pulled backward, tipping your center of gravity toward the open stairs behind you—the most dangerous direction to fall. A handrail that inches slightly ahead, by contrast, gently nudges posture upright or slightly forward, where knees and ankles can catch a stumble easily. (19), building codes typically allow handrails to run up to two percent faster than steps, while forbidding them to run noticeably slower.

What feels like a minor mechanical mismatch actually reflects (20).
passage.translation: 長い地下鉄のエスカレーターで手すりを握っていると、20秒ほど経つうちに手が体より数センチ前に進んでおり、握り直した経験がある人は多いでしょう。調整不良だと思われがちですが、実は多くのエスカレーターではゴム製の手すりが金属製のステップより1〜2％ほど速く動くよう調整されています。理由の一つは機械的な摩耗です。ステップは滑らない歯車チェーンで駆動される一方、ゴムの手すりは滑らかなローラーの摩擦で引っ張られるため、経年摩耗でわずかに滑って遅くなりやすく、新品時に少し速めにしておくことで数か月後の遅れを防いでいます。(18)、安全研究者はこの「わずかに前へ進む設定」には人間のバランスに関わる重要な理由もあると指摘します。傾斜30度で上るステップより手すりが遅いと、腕が徐々に後ろへ引かれて重心が背後の階段側——最も転落が危険な方向——へ傾いてしまいます。反対に手すりがほんの少し先行すれば姿勢は自然と直立かやや前傾になり、万一つまずいても膝や足首で踏ん張りやすくなります。(19)、建築基準では手すりがステップより最大2％速く動くことは認められる一方、目立って遅くなることは禁じられています。ちょっとしたズレに思える現象には、実は(20)が込められているのです。

passage.title: How Agroforestry Shades Coffee Crops Under Warming Skies
passage.text:
Coffee drinkers rarely picture tall banana palms, nitrogen-fixing acacia trees, and timber hardwoods growing right inside a coffee field. During the late twentieth century, many commercial estates cleared overhead trees so densely planted "sun-grown" coffee bushes, fed with heavy fertilizer, could produce maximum short-term yields.

As tropical dry seasons grow hotter and more erratic, however, full-sun coffee monocultures are showing severe strain. Arabica coffee evolved as an understory shrub in cool Ethiopian cloud forests; exposed to scorching afternoon sun above thirty degrees Celsius, its leaves close their pores, berries ripen too fast, and bean flavor turns flat and bitter. Reintroducing a dappled canopy of shade trees cools leaf temperatures by three to five degrees, letting berries mature slowly into sweeter, denser beans. (21), fallen tree leaves build a thick organic mulch that holds rainwater in the soil weeks longer.

Shade canopies diversify farm income and wildlife habitat simultaneously. While coffee is harvested once a year, fruit, avocados, and sustainably pruned firewood from canopy trees provide food and cash during lean months. Migratory songbirds patrolling the branches devour coffee berry borer beetles, reducing pesticide bills. (22), maximum coffee tonnage per hectare may dip slightly compared with heavily fertilized sun plots, yet lower input costs and specialty-grade bean prices often leave farming families more financially resilient.

Returning trees to coffee hillsides shows how traditional ecological structure can offer (23).
passage.translation: コーヒーを飲む人の多くは、コーヒー畑の中に背の高いバナナや窒素を固定するアカシア、木材用の広葉樹が一緒に生えている光景をあまり想像しないかもしれません。20世紀後半には短期的な収量を最大化するため、多くの大規模農園が頭上の木々を伐採し、大量の肥料を与えて密植する「日向栽培」へと切り替えました。しかし熱帯の乾季がより暑く不規則になるにつれ、日向の単一栽培には深刻なひずみが出ています。アラビカ種はもともとエチオピアの涼しい雲霧林の下草として進化した植物であり、30度を超える午後の直射日光にさらされると気孔を閉じ、実が早熟になって風味が平板で苦くなってしまいます。木漏れ日を作る日陰樹（シェードツリー）を戻すと葉の温度が3〜5度下がり、実がゆっくり熟して甘みと密度の高い豆になるうえ、(21)、落ち葉が厚い腐葉土となって雨水を何週間も長く土壌に保ちます。さらに樹冠の木々は農家の収入と野生生物の生息地も多様化させます。年1回収穫のコーヒーの端境期に果物やアボカド、薪が食料と現金をもたらし、枝を巡る渡り鳥が害虫を食べて農薬代を減らします。(22)、化学肥料漬けの日向畑に比べればヘクタールあたりの総重量はわずかに減る場合があるものの、資材費の削減とスペシャルティ品質の高値によって農家経営の安定性はむしろ高まります。丘に木々を取り戻すアグロフォレストリーは、(23)ことを示しています。

passage.title: How Agroforestry Shades Coffee Crops Under Warming Skies
passage.text:
Coffee drinkers rarely picture tall banana palms, nitrogen-fixing acacia trees, and timber hardwoods growing right inside a coffee field. During the late twentieth century, many commercial estates cleared overhead trees so densely planted "sun-grown" coffee bushes, fed with heavy fertilizer, could produce maximum short-term yields.

As tropical dry seasons grow hotter and more erratic, however, full-sun coffee monocultures are showing severe strain. Arabica coffee evolved as an understory shrub in cool Ethiopian cloud forests; exposed to scorching afternoon sun above thirty degrees Celsius, its leaves close their pores, berries ripen too fast, and bean flavor turns flat and bitter. Reintroducing a dappled canopy of shade trees cools leaf temperatures by three to five degrees, letting berries mature slowly into sweeter, denser beans. (21), fallen tree leaves build a thick organic mulch that holds rainwater in the soil weeks longer.

Shade canopies diversify farm income and wildlife habitat simultaneously. While coffee is harvested once a year, fruit, avocados, and sustainably pruned firewood from canopy trees provide food and cash during lean months. Migratory songbirds patrolling the branches devour coffee berry borer beetles, reducing pesticide bills. (22), maximum coffee tonnage per hectare may dip slightly compared with heavily fertilized sun plots, yet lower input costs and specialty-grade bean prices often leave farming families more financially resilient.

Returning trees to coffee hillsides shows how traditional ecological structure can offer (23).
passage.translation: コーヒーを飲む人の多くは、コーヒー畑の中に背の高いバナナや窒素を固定するアカシア、木材用の広葉樹が一緒に生えている光景をあまり想像しないかもしれません。20世紀後半には短期的な収量を最大化するため、多くの大規模農園が頭上の木々を伐採し、大量の肥料を与えて密植する「日向栽培」へと切り替えました。しかし熱帯の乾季がより暑く不規則になるにつれ、日向の単一栽培には深刻なひずみが出ています。アラビカ種はもともとエチオピアの涼しい雲霧林の下草として進化した植物であり、30度を超える午後の直射日光にさらされると気孔を閉じ、実が早熟になって風味が平板で苦くなってしまいます。木漏れ日を作る日陰樹（シェードツリー）を戻すと葉の温度が3〜5度下がり、実がゆっくり熟して甘みと密度の高い豆になるうえ、(21)、落ち葉が厚い腐葉土となって雨水を何週間も長く土壌に保ちます。さらに樹冠の木々は農家の収入と野生生物の生息地も多様化させます。年1回収穫のコーヒーの端境期に果物やアボカド、薪が食料と現金をもたらし、枝を巡る渡り鳥が害虫を食べて農薬代を減らします。(22)、化学肥料漬けの日向畑に比べればヘクタールあたりの総重量はわずかに減る場合があるものの、資材費の削減とスペシャルティ品質の高値によって農家経営の安定性はむしろ高まります。丘に木々を取り戻すアグロフォレストリーは、(23)ことを示しています。

passage.title: Instructions for Costume Dyeing Workshop Participants
passage.text:
From: Indigo Craft Studio "Aizome-Kobo"
To: Saturday Workshop Participants
Subject: Clothing preparation and fabric limits for natural indigo dyeing

Dear participants,
We are delighted that you will join our natural sukumo indigo dyeing workshop this Saturday from 1:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. In addition to the plain cotton tenugui towel included in your fee, each participant may bring ONE personal garment from home to dye in the vats.

Please check the care label of your item carefully tonight: natural plant fibers—100% cotton, linen, or hemp—absorb indigo beautifully, whereas polyester, nylon, and acrylic threads repel natural dye and will remain white, leaving uneven blotches around seams. Even a brand-new 100% cotton T-shirt is coated with invisible factory starch that blocks dye, so you MUST wash your garment in warm water with mild detergent (no fabric softener!) and bring it clean and dry.

Keep the dry weight of your personal item under 250 grams—roughly one adult T-shirt or light tote bag. Heavy denim jeans or thick hoodies soak up too much vat liquid and exhaust the dye bath for others. Long rubber gloves and aprons are provided at the studio.

Warmly,
Aizome-Kobo Team
passage.translation: 藍染工房から土曜ワークショップ参加者への連絡。今週土曜午後1時〜4時の天然すくも藍染め体験では、参加費に含まれる無地の木綿手ぬぐいに加え、自宅から各自1点だけ衣類等を持参して染められる。今夜のうちに洗濯表示をよく確認すること：綿・麻100％などの天然植物繊維は美しく染まるが、ポリエステル・ナイロン・アクリル糸は天然染料をはじいて白いまま残り、縫い目などがまだらになる。また新品の綿100％Tシャツにも染料を妨げる目に見えない工場の糊がついているため、必ず事前にぬるま湯と中性洗剤（柔軟剤は使用不可）で洗って乾かした清潔な状態で持参すること。持参品の乾燥重量は250グラム以下（大人用Tシャツ1枚または薄手トートバッグ程度）に抑えること。重いデニムや厚手パーカーは染液を吸いすぎて他の参加者の分を弱めてしまう。長いゴム手袋とエプロンは工房で用意する。

passage.title: How Quiet Asphalt Reduces Highway Tire Roar
passage.text:
Stand beside a suburban expressway where cars cruise at eighty kilometers per hour, and you might assume engines and exhaust pipes create most of the noise. For passenger cars built over the past twenty years, however, tire-pavement noise actually overtakes engine sound once speeds pass roughly forty to fifty kilometers per hour—a fact made even clearer as quiet electric vehicles still produce a steady roar at highway speeds.

Much of that highway roar comes from "air pumping." As a spinning rubber tire flattens against smooth, dense asphalt, air trapped inside the tire's tread grooves is squeezed violently and shoots out to the sides like thousands of tiny whistles per second, amplified by the curved horn shape between tire and road. On rain-slicked dense pavement, surface water also sprays upward, reducing driver visibility and increasing hydroplaning risk.

Road engineers in the Netherlands, Japan, and Scandinavia developed an effective acoustic remedy: porous elastic road surfaces, often called "quiet asphalt." By leaving out fine sand particles and binding coarse crushed stone with polymer-modified bitumen, crews lay a top wearing course riddled with interconnected tiny air voids—roughly twenty percent open pore space. Instead of squirting sideways with a hiss, compressed air under the tire escapes harmlessly downward into the porous mat. Rainwater drains straight through those same channels to roadside gutters, cutting splash spray dramatically.

Porous asphalt comes with real upkeep trade-offs, though. Dust, tire rubber crumbs, and autumn mud gradually clog the tiny pores within five to eight years unless specialized high-pressure vacuum trucks flush them clean. In snowy mountain passes, water freezing inside clogged pores can loosen stones under snowplow blades.

Even with shorter resurfacing cycles, cities bordering busy ring roads value porous pavements highly: cutting traffic noise by four to six decibels sounds to the human ear much like cutting traffic volume in half.
passage.translation: 時速80キロで車が流れる郊外の幹線道路脇に立つと、騒音の大半はエンジンやマフラーから出ていると思いがちです。しかし過去20年間に作られた乗用車では、時速40〜50キロを超えると実際にはタイヤと路面の摩擦音がエンジン音を上回ります。静かな電気自動車でも高速走行時にゴーッという連続音が出る事実がそれをよく物語っています。この高速道路騒音の大きな原因は「エアポンピング現象」です。回転するゴムタイヤが緻密で平らなアスファルトに押しつけられると、溝に閉じ込められた空気が激しく圧縮されて横へ噴き出し、タイヤと路面の隙間で増幅されて毎秒何千もの小さな笛のような音を生むのです。そこでオランダや日本、北欧の道路技術者が実用化したのが、細かい砂を抜いて粗い砕石を改質アスファルトで固め、約20％の連続した微細な空隙を持たせた「排水性（低騒音）舗装」です。タイヤ下の圧縮空気が横へ噴き出す代わりに舗装内部の隙間へ逃げるため音が静まり、雨水もそのまま路肩へ排水されるため水しぶきやハイドロプレーニングも劇的に減ります。もっとも5〜8年で砂塵などが隙間を詰まらせるため専用高圧洗浄車での清掃が欠かせず、豪雪地帯では凍結や除雪板による骨材飛散の課題もありますが、騒音を4〜6デシベル下げる効果は人間の耳には交通量がほぼ半減したかのように感じられるため、都市の環状道路沿いで高く評価されています。

passage.title: How Quiet Asphalt Reduces Highway Tire Roar
passage.text:
Stand beside a suburban expressway where cars cruise at eighty kilometers per hour, and you might assume engines and exhaust pipes create most of the noise. For passenger cars built over the past twenty years, however, tire-pavement noise actually overtakes engine sound once speeds pass roughly forty to fifty kilometers per hour—a fact made even clearer as quiet electric vehicles still produce a steady roar at highway speeds.

Much of that highway roar comes from "air pumping." As a spinning rubber tire flattens against smooth, dense asphalt, air trapped inside the tire's tread grooves is squeezed violently and shoots out to the sides like thousands of tiny whistles per second, amplified by the curved horn shape between tire and road. On rain-slicked dense pavement, surface water also sprays upward, reducing driver visibility and increasing hydroplaning risk.

Road engineers in the Netherlands, Japan, and Scandinavia developed an effective acoustic remedy: porous elastic road surfaces, often called "quiet asphalt." By leaving out fine sand particles and binding coarse crushed stone with polymer-modified bitumen, crews lay a top wearing course riddled with interconnected tiny air voids—roughly twenty percent open pore space. Instead of squirting sideways with a hiss, compressed air under the tire escapes harmlessly downward into the porous mat. Rainwater drains straight through those same channels to roadside gutters, cutting splash spray dramatically.

Porous asphalt comes with real upkeep trade-offs, though. Dust, tire rubber crumbs, and autumn mud gradually clog the tiny pores within five to eight years unless specialized high-pressure vacuum trucks flush them clean. In snowy mountain passes, water freezing inside clogged pores can loosen stones under snowplow blades.

Even with shorter resurfacing cycles, cities bordering busy ring roads value porous pavements highly: cutting traffic noise by four to six decibels sounds to the human ear much like cutting traffic volume in half.

passage.title: Why Escalator Steps Have Deep Grooves Along Their Treads
passage.text:
Look down at the moving metal steps of any train-station escalator, and you will see dozens of narrow parallel ridges and grooves running from back to front—never side to side. Passengers sometimes assume those grooves exist mainly to give wet sneakers extra grip on rainy days. While texture does help drainage, mechanical engineers designed those deep longitudinal cleats primarily so the steps can disappear safely at the end of the ride.

At the top and bottom landings of an escalator, moving steps slide beneath a stationary metal plate edged with sharp teeth, called the "comb plate." Those comb teeth mesh right inside the grooves of each passing step with less than two millimeters to spare. Instead of hitting a flat edge where shoe soles, umbrella tips, or wheeled luggage could catch, passengers glide smoothly off the ridges onto the solid floor. (18), small objects like gravel or dropped coins are scooped upward onto the landing rather than dragged down into the return machinery.

Keeping that comb-and-groove partnership safe requires watchful upkeep. If a heavy steel cart chips even two adjacent comb teeth, a dangerous snagging gap opens up. Modern escalators wire sensitive switches behind the comb plate that halt the motor instantly if anything jams under a tooth. (19), yellow painted borders frame each tread to warn riders away from the hinge seams between steps.

Every detail of an escalator step shows how everyday transit hardware (20).

passage.title: Why Escalator Steps Have Deep Grooves Along Their Treads
passage.text:
Look down at the moving metal steps of any train-station escalator, and you will see dozens of narrow parallel ridges and grooves running from back to front—never side to side. Passengers sometimes assume those grooves exist mainly to give wet sneakers extra grip on rainy days. While texture does help drainage, mechanical engineers designed those deep longitudinal cleats primarily so the steps can disappear safely at the end of the ride.

At the top and bottom landings of an escalator, moving steps slide beneath a stationary metal plate edged with sharp teeth, called the "comb plate." Those comb teeth mesh right inside the grooves of each passing step with less than two millimeters to spare. Instead of hitting a flat edge where shoe soles, umbrella tips, or wheeled luggage could catch, passengers glide smoothly off the ridges onto the solid floor. (18), small objects like gravel or dropped coins are scooped upward onto the landing rather than dragged down into the return machinery.

Keeping that comb-and-groove partnership safe requires watchful upkeep. If a heavy steel cart chips even two adjacent comb teeth, a dangerous snagging gap opens up. Modern escalators wire sensitive switches behind the comb plate that halt the motor instantly if anything jams under a tooth. (19), yellow painted borders frame each tread to warn riders away from the hinge seams between steps.

Every detail of an escalator step shows how everyday transit hardware (20).

passage.title: How Community Tool Libraries Cut Waste and Build Skills
passage.text:
Walk down the hardware aisle of a home-improvement store, and you will see high-pressure washers, tile cutters, post-hole diggers, and orbital sanders gleaming on the shelves. Useful as these machines are during a weekend renovation, industry surveys suggest the average household power drill runs for fewer than thirty minutes across its entire lifetime before sitting idle in a garage.

Recognizing the absurdity of fifty neighbors on one street each owning an identical ladder that gathers dust, residents in cities from Portland and Edinburgh to Kyoto have launched nonprofit "tool libraries." For a modest annual membership—often less than the cost of buying a single saw—members check out commercial-grade tools for a week just like library books. Sharing one sturdy sander among forty households cuts raw manufacturing demand for copper motors, lithium packs, and molded plastic housings. (21), apartment dwellers without garages can tackle home repairs they once had to postpone.

Tool libraries quickly discover that lending hardware is only half their value. Beginners borrowing a sewing machine or circular saw for the first time need safe habits, so retired cabinetmakers and electricians volunteer on Saturday mornings to teach hands-on safety clinics. (22), neighbors swap leftover paint, spare screws, and practical advice over workbenches.

Not every item suits shared lending—cheap paintbrushes wear out fast—yet pooling durable equipment offers neighborhoods (23).
passage.translation: ホームセンターの工具売り場を歩けば、高圧洗浄機やタイルカッター、電動サンダーが棚に並んでいます。週末の模様替えには頼もしい機械ですが、業界調査によると一般家庭の電動ドリルが生涯で実際に回る時間は合計30分にも満たず、大半の時間はガレージで眠っています。同じ通りの50世帯がそれぞれほこりをかぶる脚立を1台ずつ所有する無駄に気づいた住民たちは、ポートランドやエディンバラ、京都などの都市で非営利の「工具図書館」を始めました。のこぎり1本分にも満たない手頃な年会費でプロ仕様の工具を1週間借りられ、頑丈なサンダー1台を40世帯で共有すれば銅モーターやリチウム電池、樹脂筐体の製造資源を減らせます。(21)、収納場所のない集合住宅の住民も先延ばしにしていた修繕に取り組めます。さらに初心者向けに退職した家具職人や電気技師が土曜午前に安全講習を開くようになり、(22)、作業台越しに余った塗料やネジ、実用的な知恵も交換されています。消耗の激しい安価な刷毛などは向きませんが、丈夫な機材を持ち寄る仕組みは地域に(23)をもたらしています。

passage.title: Instructions for Participating in the River Salmon Fry Release
passage.text:
From: Kitagawa Watershed Conservation Association
To: Registered Families and High School Volunteers
Subject: Bucket acclimatization rule for Sunday's salmon fry release

Dear participants,
Thank you for joining our annual chum salmon fry release at Kitagawa River Park this Sunday at 10:00 a.m.! Over the winter, student volunteers tended fertilized eggs in chilled hatchery trays, and twelve thousand five-centimeter young salmon are now ready to begin their journey to the Pacific.

When you receive your small plastic bucket of fry at the riverside tent, please do NOT pour the fish straight into the river right away. Hatchery tank water is nine degrees Celsius, whereas sunlit river shallows may be three degrees warmer or cooler; a sudden temperature shock stuns tiny fish and leaves them vulnerable to birds.

Instead, crouch safely at the gravel edge, dip half your bucket into the river to mix river water in gradually over two minutes, and then tilt the rim gently underwater so the fry swim out on their own. Life jackets will be lent to all children under twelve.

Kitagawa Conservation Staff
passage.translation: 北川流域保全協会から登録家族・高校生ボランティアへのメール。今週日曜午前10時からの北川河川公園でのサケ稚魚放流会では、冬の間ボランティアがふ化槽で育てた体長5センチの稚魚1万2千匹を海へ送り出す。河原のテントで稚魚入りのバケツを受け取ったら、すぐに川へ流し込まないこと。ふ化槽の水は9度だが日差しの当たる浅瀬は3度前後高い（または低い）ことがあり、急激な水温変化は小さな魚にショックを与えて鳥に狙われやすくしてしまう。安全な砂利岸にしゃがみ、2分間かけて川の水を少しずつバケツに混ぜて水温をなじませてから、縁を水中にそっと傾けて稚魚が自力で泳ぎ出すようにすること。12歳未満の子ども全員にライフジャケットを貸し出す。

items.prompt: What should participants do for two minutes at the gravel edge before releasing the fry?
choices: Count all twelve thousand fish one by one.
Gradually mix river water into their bucket to equalize the temperature.
Feed bread crumbs to nearby river birds.
Warm the bucket with a portable heater.
items.explanation: dip half your bucket into the river to mix river water in gradually over two minutesとある。
distractorReasons: 1万2千匹を数えるのではない。
2分間かけて川の水を少しずつバケツに混ぜ、水温をなじませる。
鳥にパンをやるのは逆効果。
ヒーター加熱ではない。
items.translation: 稚魚を放す前、砂利の岸辺で2分間何をすべきですか。

Hatchery tank water is nine degrees Celsius, whereas sunlit river shallows may be three degrees warmer or cooler; a sudden temperature shock stuns tiny fish and leaves them vulnerable to birds.

Instead, crouch safely at the gravel edge, dip half your bucket into the river to mix river water in gradually over two minutes, and then tilt the rim gently underwater so the fry swim out on their own. Life jackets will be lent to all children under twelve.

Kitagawa Conservation Staff
passage.translation: 北川流域保全協会から登録家族・高校生ボランティアへのメール。今週日曜午前10時からの北川河川公園でのサケ稚魚放流会では、冬の間ボランティアがふ化槽で育てた体長5センチの稚魚1万2千匹を海へ送り出す。河原のテントで稚魚入りのバケツを受け取ったら、すぐに川へ流し込まないこと。ふ化槽の水は9度だが日差しの当たる浅瀬は3度前後高い（または低い）ことがあり、急激な水温変化は小さな魚にショックを与えて鳥に狙われやすくしてしまう。安全な砂利岸にしゃがみ、2分間かけて川の水を少しずつバケツに混ぜて水温をなじませてから、縁を水中にそっと傾けて稚魚が自力で泳ぎ出すようにすること。12歳未満の子ども全員にライフジャケットを貸し出す。

items.prompt: Why are galleries showing woodblock prints, textiles, or watercolors kept noticeably dim?
choices: Light triggers chemical reactions that permanently fade organic dyes and weaken paper or silk.
Museums turn off half their lamps to lower summer power bills.
Visitors prefer guessing colors in the dark.
Oil paintings and glazed ceramics melt at normal office brightness.
items.explanation: light itself is an invisible chemical force that permanently fades organic pigments and weakens paper fibersとある。
distractorReasons: 第1・2段落の理由と一致。
節電ではないと第1段落で否定されている。
暗闇で色を当てさせるためではない。
油絵や陶器は比較的強いと対比されている。
items.translation: 木版画や染織品、水彩画を展示する部屋が目立って薄暗く保たれているのはなぜですか。

passage.title: Why Museums Control Light Exposure with Strict "Lux Budgets"
passage.text:
Step from a sunlit sculpture court into a gallery displaying Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints, medieval illuminated manuscripts, or nineteenth-century watercolor landscapes, and the room can feel surprisingly dim—almost like twilight. Visitors occasionally wonder whether the museum is cutting electricity costs. Conservators have a far more urgent motive: light itself is an invisible chemical force that permanently fades organic pigments and weakens paper fibers.

Unlike oil paintings on canvas or glazed ceramics—whose mineral pigments locked in linseed oil or glass tolerate moderate museum lighting well—plant dyes, insect inks, silk threads, and watercolor washes contain fragile molecular bonds. Photons of light, especially high-energy ultraviolet rays and blue wavelengths, snap those bonds one by one. Worse still, photochemical damage is strictly cumulative and irreversible: exposing a delicate Hiroshige print to bright gallery lamps for one week causes roughly the same fading as ten weeks under lamps one-tenth as bright, and no rest in a dark vault afterward can bring lost blues or purples back.

To balance public enjoyment today against preservation for centuries ahead, major museums manage fragile works under an annual "lux-hour budget." Illuminance is capped at just fifty lux—roughly a fifth of normal office brightness—with all ultraviolet filtered out. Curators also track how many hours each print spends on display; once a work reaches its yearly allowance, say three months, it returns to dark climate-controlled storage while a companion print takes its place.

Modern LEDs free of ultraviolet heat, paired with motion sensors or velvet curtains that visitors lift briefly inside display cases, stretch those precious light budgets further than ever.

Dim rooms and rotating exhibitions may test a visitor's patience, yet they ensure our grandchildren will still see the artist's original colors rather than pale ghosts.
passage.translation: 日差しの入る彫刻庭園から日本の浮世絵版画や中世の彩飾写本、19世紀の水彩画が並ぶ展示室へ足を踏み入れると、夕暮れのように薄暗く感じることがあります。節電かと思われがちですが、保存修復家には切実な理由があります。光そのものが有機顔料を退色させ紙や絹の繊維を弱める目に見えない化学作用を持つからです。油絵具や陶磁器の釉薬に守られた鉱物顔料と違い、植物染料や水彩絵具の分子結合は紫外線や青色光によって少しずつ切断されます。しかも光による損傷は「累積的かつ不可逆的」であり、強い光に1週間さらすのも10分の1の光に10週間さらすのも同程度の退色を招き、あとから暗室で休ませても失われた青や紫は二度と戻りません。そこで美術館は照度を50ルクス程度に抑え紫外線を除去したうえで「年間積算照度（ルクス時）の予算」を定め、3か月ほど展示したら収蔵庫へ戻して別の作品と入れ替えています。紫外線を出さないLEDや人感センサーも活用されており、薄暗い展示室と展示替えは未来の世代に本来の色彩を残すための知恵なのです。

items.prompt: What does the author mean by saying light damage to fragile pigments is "cumulative and irreversible"?
choices: Only sunlight from open windows causes fading, never indoor lamps.
Colors fade during winter but grow brighter again every August.
Fading adds up with total light exposure over time, and storing a print in the dark cannot restore lost colors.
Prints suffer zero damage as long as museum rooms stay below twenty degrees.
items.explanation: 総受光量に応じて損傷が積み重なり（明るい1週間＝10分の1の10週間）、あとで暗い収蔵庫に置いても失われた色は戻らない。
distractorReasons: 室内灯でも起きる。
8月に色が戻ることはない。
第2段落後半の説明と完全一致。
低温でも光損傷は起きる。
items.translation: 壊れやすい顔料への光損傷が「累積的で不可逆的」だとはどういう意味ですか。

items.prompt: How does an annual "lux-hour budget" work in museum practice?
choices: Every painting is repainted with fresh blue dye once a year.
Visitors pay fifty yen per hour to rent flashlights.
Museums display all prints outdoors on cloudy days only.
Curators limit brightness to around fifty lux and rotate fragile works back into dark storage after a set display period.
items.explanation: 照度を約50ルクス以下に抑え、展示時間を記録して年間上限（例：3か月）に達したら暗所の空調収蔵庫へ戻して別作品と入れ替える。
distractorReasons: 毎年の塗り直しではない。
懐中電灯の有料貸出ではない。
曇天屋外展示ではない。
第3段落の運用説明と一致。
items.translation: 美術館の実務における年間の「ルクス時予算」はどのように機能していますか。

items.prompt: How do motion sensors or small curtains over display cases help conservators?
choices: They warm ancient silk threads to forty degrees.
They keep dust and insects out of oil paintings.
They cut unnecessary light exposure when nobody is looking directly at the artwork.
They photograph visitors who stand too close.
items.explanation: 誰も見ていない時間の不要な露光を減らし、貴重な年間露光枠を長持ちさせる（stretch those precious light budgets further）。
distractorReasons: 40度加熱ではない。
油絵の防虫目的ではない。
第4段落の技術的工夫と一致。
来館者撮影ではない。
items.translation: 人感センサーや展示ケースの小カーテンは保存修復家をどのように助けますか。

Modern LEDs allow fragile prints to stay under bright spotlights forever.
Grandchildren prefer pale faded prints over vivid ones.

最終段落の主張と完全一致。
LEDでも無制限に強い光を当てられるわけではない。
退色した版画を好むのではない。
items.translation: 最終段落における筆者の主張は何ですか。

items.prompt: To keep invasive seeds from spreading between islands, hikers must (     ) mud off their boot soles before boarding the boat.
items.explanation: 島の間で外来植物の種が広がるのを防ぐため、乗船前に靴底の泥をブラシで「こすり落とす」scrub。
distractorReasons: scrub mud off ... で泥をこすり落とす。
scribbleは走り書きする。
scrambleはよじ登る・かき混ぜる。
scorchは焦がす。
items.translation: 島々の間で外来種の種子が広がるのを防ぐため、登山者は船に乗る前に靴底の泥をこすり落とさなければなりません。

items.prompt: The two coastal villages look peaceful today, yet archive records show they once competed (     ) for herring fishing rights.
items.explanation: 今は穏やかに見える2つの漁村だが、かつてはニシン漁業権をめぐって「激しく」競い合っていたcompeted fiercely。
distractorReasons: fondlyは懐かしく。
faintlyはかすかに。
compete fiercelyで激しく争う・競争する。peaceful todayとの対比に合致。
fluentlyは流暢に。
items.translation: その2つの海辺の村は今では穏やかに見えますが、古文書によるとかつてはニシンの漁業権をめぐって激しく競い合っていました。

items.prompt: Because handmade violin varnish dries slowly, luthiers refrain from (     ) a second coat until the first feels completely firm.
items.explanation: 手作りのバイオリン用ニスは乾きが遅いため、1層目が完全に固まるまで2層目を「塗る」のを控えるapplying a second coat。
distractorReasons: appealは訴える。
apply a coat of varnishでニスをひと塗りする。
appointは任命する。
approveは承認する。
items.translation: 手づくりのバイオリン用ニスは乾くのが遅いため、弦楽器職人は1層目が完全に固まるまで2層目を塗るのを控えます。

items.prompt: The municipal observatory lent solar-filter glasses to elementary schools (     ) Tuesday's partial eclipse.
items.explanation: 火曜日の部分日食「に先立って・の前に」小学校へ日食グラスを貸し出したahead of。
distractorReasons: alongside ofはこの時の表現に使わない。
apart fromは〜は別として。
aside fromも〜を除いて。
ahead of Tuesday's eclipseで日食に先立って。
items.translation: 火曜日の部分日食に先立ち、市立天文台は市内の小学校に太陽観測用グラスを貸し出しました。

items.prompt: When frost heaved the brick garden path uneven, Grandpa had the loose bricks (     ) on a fresh bed of sand.
items.explanation: 霜柱でレンガの小道がでこぼこに浮き上がった際、緩んだレンガを新しい砂床の上に「敷き直してもらった」had the loose bricks relaid（relayの過去分詞）。
distractorReasons: relay bricks（レンガを敷き直す）の過去分詞relaid。
reliedはrely（頼る）の過去分詞。
relievedは和らげた。
rehearsedはリハーサルした。
items.translation: 霜で庭のレンガ道がでこぼこに浮き上がったとき、祖父は新しい砂の層の上に浮いたレンガを敷き直してもらいました。

items.prompt: Although automated translation handles menus well, diplomats remain (     ) to rely on software during delicate treaty talks.
items.explanation: 繊細な条約交渉の場ではソフトに頼ることに「消極的である・ためらいがある」remain reluctant to do。
distractorReasons: redundantは余剰の。
reluctant to doで〜するのをためらう・気が進まない。
relevantは関連がある。
radiantは輝くばかりの。

items.prompt: Adding crushed oyster shells to acidic farm soil helps restore the mineral (     ) needed by spinach roots.

passage.title: Why Bakery Ovens Inject Steam During the First Minutes of Baking
passage.text:
Home cooks trying to recreate a crackling, glossy artisan baguette in an ordinary kitchen oven often run into the same disappointment: although the dough tastes fine, the crust comes out thick, dull gray-brown, and tough to chew rather than thin, blistered, and golden. Ask a professional baker what made the difference, and the answer is rarely secret flour—it is a burst of hot steam injected right as the loaves hit the stone.

Steam transforms crust chemistry during the critical first five minutes before the dough's outer skin sets. When invisible water vapor condenses onto the cooler surface of raw dough, it keeps the outer starch layer moist and elastic. That brief elasticity allows expanding carbon dioxide inside to stretch the loaf to full, airy volume without tearing prematurely. (18), moisture dissolves surface starches into a thin glaze that caramelizes into a crisp, shiny amber sheen once dry heat takes over.

Leaving steam on for the entire bake would produce soggy bread, of course. Commercial deck ovens therefore vent the humid air out halfway through baking so dry heat can crisp the exterior. Dedicated home bakers mimic this two-stage process by baking loaves inside a preheated cast-iron pot with a tight lid for twenty minutes—trapping the dough's own moisture—before removing the lid to brown. (19), even standard home ovens can turn out bakery-worthy loaves.

Managing moisture alongside heat illustrates how small shifts in timing (20).
passage.translation: 家庭の一般的なオーブンでパリッと艶のある本格的なバゲットを焼こうとすると、味は悪くないのに皮が分厚くくすんだ茶色になり、薄く香ばしい黄金色にならないことがよくあります。プロのパン職人に違いを尋ねれば、秘密の小麦粉ではなく「生地を窯に入れた直後に吹き込む熱い蒸気」だという答えが返ってきます。蒸気は表面が固まる前の最初の5分間に皮の化学変化を一変させます。水蒸気が冷たい生生地の表面で結露すると外側のデンプン層がしっとりと伸びやかになり、内部の炭酸ガスが表面を早く破ることなくパンをふっくら最大まで膨らませます。(18)、溶けた表面のデンプンが薄い糊の層となり、後半の乾いた熱でパリッとした琥珀色の艶へとキャラメル化します。もちろん最後まで蒸気を残せばべたつくため、業務用オーブンは途中で蒸気を逃がします。熱く予熱した鋳物ホーロー鍋に蓋をして20分焼き、生地自身の水分を閉じ込めてから蓋を外す方法をとれば、(19)、家庭の普通のオーブンでも専門店顔負けのパンが焼けます。熱とともに水分を操る工夫は、タイミングの小さな違いがいかに(20)かを示しています。

passage.title: How Beaver Dams Restore Drying Mountain Meadows
passage.text:
Across western North America and parts of Europe, summer streamflows in mountain valleys have grown more erratic as winter snowpacks melt weeks earlier in spring. Streams that once meandered slowly across lush wet meadows now rush down eroded gullies in April, leaving valleys parched and fire-prone by August. To hold precious snowmelt higher in watersheds, land managers are enlisting a furry native engineer once trapped as a nuisance: the beaver.

Where beavers return—or where conservation crews weave starter "beaver dam analogs" from willow posts to invite them back—the landscape transforms within two seasons. Gnawing small streamside aspens and packing mud against branches, a single beaver family builds leaky stick dams that slow rushing water into stair-stepped ponds. Water spreads sideways into floodplain soils, raising the local water table by up to a meter. (21), cold groundwater seeps back into the creek gradually through late summer, keeping downstream trout cool during heat waves.

Satellite photos of recent western wildfires revealed a dramatic bonus. While surrounding dry pine ridges burned black, wide emerald ribbons of beaver-irrigated willow marsh stayed too wet to ignite, offering safe refuge for deer, amphibians, and songbirds. (22), beaver ponds trap silt and ash washed down after storms, protecting town drinking-water intakes farther downstream.

Coexisting with beavers near roads requires simple culvert guards so ponds don't flood highways, yet working alongside nature's builders offers (23).
passage.translation: 北米西部や欧州の一部では、春の雪解けが数週間早まったことで山あいの夏の河川流量が不安定になり、かつて湿原をゆっくり蛇行していた小川が4月に一気に流れ下って8月には乾燥し山火事の危険を高めています。貴重な雪解け水を上流にとどめるため、流域管理者が再び力を借りているのが、かつて害獣として捕獲されていた在来の土木技師・ビーバーです。ビーバーが戻る（あるいはヤナギの杭で呼び水となる簡易ダムを組む）と、わずか2季節で景観は一変します。枝と泥で築かれた適度に水を通すダムが急流を階段状の池に変え、水が横の土壌へ広がって地下水位を最大1メートル押し上げます。(21)、冷たい地下水が晩夏にかけて少しずつ川へしみ出し、猛暑の中でも下流のマスを守ります。さらに近年の山火事の衛星写真では、周囲の乾いた尾根が黒焦げになる中、ビーバーが潤したヤナギ湿地が緑の防火帯となってシカや両生類の避難場所となり、(22)、大雨後の土砂や灰も池が受け止めて下流の町の上水取水口を守ることが分かりました。道路脇の排水管ガードなどの小さな工夫を添えれば、自然の建築家との協働は(23)をもたらします。

passage.title: How Beaver Dams Restore Drying Mountain Meadows
passage.text:
Across western North America and parts of Europe, summer streamflows in mountain valleys have grown more erratic as winter snowpacks melt weeks earlier in spring. Streams that once meandered slowly across lush wet meadows now rush down eroded gullies in April, leaving valleys parched and fire-prone by August. To hold precious snowmelt higher in watersheds, land managers are enlisting a furry native engineer once trapped as a nuisance: the beaver.

Where beavers return—or where conservation crews weave starter "beaver dam analogs" from willow posts to invite them back—the landscape transforms within two seasons. Gnawing small streamside aspens and packing mud against branches, a single beaver family builds leaky stick dams that slow rushing water into stair-stepped ponds. Water spreads sideways into floodplain soils, raising the local water table by up to a meter. (21), cold groundwater seeps back into the creek gradually through late summer, keeping downstream trout cool during heat waves.

Satellite photos of recent western wildfires revealed a dramatic bonus. While surrounding dry pine ridges burned black, wide emerald ribbons of beaver-irrigated willow marsh stayed too wet to ignite, offering safe refuge for deer, amphibians, and songbirds. (22), beaver ponds trap silt and ash washed down after storms, protecting town drinking-water intakes farther downstream.

Coexisting with beavers near roads requires simple culvert guards so ponds don't flood highways, yet working alongside nature's builders offers (23).

Camp Safety Coordinator

passage.title: Modular Wood Construction in Mid-Rise Buildings
passage.text:
Mention wooden buildings, and most city dwellers picture one- or two-story houses framed with slender timber studs. Steel and concrete dominated urban skylines throughout the twentieth century for obvious reasons: ordinary sawn boards warp, shrink, and burn too readily to support ten- or fifteen-story apartments safely. Over the past two decades, however, an engineered material called cross-laminated timber—or CLT—has allowed architects in Austria, Norway, Canada, and Japan to erect quiet, sturdy wooden offices and dormitories rising a dozen stories or more.

CLT panels are made by kiln-drying boards of sustainably harvested spruce, cedar, or larch, stacking them in alternating ninety-degree layers like giant plywood, and pressing them together with structural adhesives. Alternating the wood grain perpendicular to each neighboring layer prevents warping and gives thick panels load-bearing strength comparable, pound for pound, to reinforced concrete—at roughly one-fifth the weight.

Fire safety, often the public's first worry, behaves quite differently in thick mass timber than in thin house framing. Whereas a camp-stove stick catches fire quickly, holding a match to a thick log barely scorches the bark. In laboratory furnace tests, the outer few centimeters of a massive CLT wall char slowly into an insulating carbon layer that shields the cool structural core inside, allowing engineers to calculate two-hour fire ratings with precision.

Factory prefabrication adds speed on crowded city streets. Computer-guided saws cut window openings and plumbing channels to millimeter accuracy indoors; numbered wall panels arrive on flatbed trucks and crane into place in days rather than months, slashing neighborhood noise and cement-mixer traffic.

Mass timber will not replace steel skyscrapers or bridge foundations, yet substituting renewable wood panels—which store carbon absorbed while trees grew—for energy-intensive concrete in mid-rise buildings offers cities a cleaner way to build.
passage.translation: 木造建築と聞くと多くの都市住民は細い柱で組まれた1〜2階建ての住宅を思い浮かべます。普通の挽き板は反りや収縮、燃焼の問題があるため20世紀の都市では鉄とコンクリートが主役でしたが、ここ20年ほどで「直交集成板（CLT）」と呼ばれるエンジニアリングウッドが登場し、オーストリアやノルウェー、カナダ、日本で10階を超える静かで頑丈な木造オフィスや学生寮が建てられるようになりました。乾燥させたスギやカラマツなどの板を繊維方向が90度ずつ直交するよう何層も重ねて接着プレスすることで反りを抑え、重量あたり鉄筋コンクリートに匹敵する強度を約5分の1の軽さで実現します。最も心配されやすい耐火性についても、太い丸太にマッチを当てても燃え広がりにくいのと同様、分厚いCLTパネルは表面の数センチがゆっくり炭化して断熱層となり内部の構造芯を守るため、2時間耐火などの性能を精密に設計できます。さらに工場でミリ単位の窓穴や配管溝まで加工して現場でクレーン組立するため工期や騒音も大幅に減り、成長中に吸収した炭素を蓄え続ける中層建築の新しい選択肢となっています。

passage.title: Modular Wood Construction in Mid-Rise Buildings
passage.text:
Mention wooden buildings, and most city dwellers picture one- or two-story houses framed with slender timber studs. Steel and concrete dominated urban skylines throughout the twentieth century for obvious reasons: ordinary sawn boards warp, shrink, and burn too readily to support ten- or fifteen-story apartments safely. Over the past two decades, however, an engineered material called cross-laminated timber—or CLT—has allowed architects in Austria, Norway, Canada, and Japan to erect quiet, sturdy wooden offices and dormitories rising a dozen stories or more.

CLT panels are made by kiln-drying boards of sustainably harvested spruce, cedar, or larch, stacking them in alternating ninety-degree layers like giant plywood, and pressing them together with structural adhesives. Alternating the wood grain perpendicular to each neighboring layer prevents warping and gives thick panels load-bearing strength comparable, pound for pound, to reinforced concrete—at roughly one-fifth the weight.

Fire safety, often the public's first worry, behaves quite differently in thick mass timber than in thin house framing. Whereas a camp-stove stick catches fire quickly, holding a match to a thick log barely scorches the bark. In laboratory furnace tests, the outer few centimeters of a massive CLT wall char slowly into an insulating carbon layer that shields the cool structural core inside, allowing engineers to calculate two-hour fire ratings with precision.

Factory prefabrication adds speed on crowded city streets. Computer-guided saws cut window openings and plumbing channels to millimeter accuracy indoors; numbered wall panels arrive on flatbed trucks and crane into place in days rather than months, slashing neighborhood noise and cement-mixer traffic.

Mass timber will not replace steel skyscrapers or bridge foundations, yet substituting renewable wood panels—which store carbon absorbed while trees grew—for energy-intensive concrete in mid-rise buildings offers cities a cleaner way to build.

passage.title: Why Supermarket Shopping Carts Have Slightly Angled Front Casters
passage.text:
Push an empty shopping cart across a smooth supermarket floor, and it glides effortlessly around tight dairy corners with one hand. Try steering a heavy four-wheeled warehouse dolly whose wheels are all locked straight, by contrast, and turning requires lifting one end off the ground. Behind the shopping cart's nimble handling—and its occasional annoying wobble—lies subtle caster-wheel geometry.

A shopping cart pairs two fixed rear wheels with two front "swivel casters" that rotate 360 degrees. Look closely at a front wheel fork, and you will see the wheel axle sits a couple of centimeters BEHIND the vertical pivot pin attached to the cart frame. Engineers call that small offset "caster trail." Whenever you push the cart forward, floor friction pulls the wheel neatly into alignment behind the pivot, much like a weathervane aligning with the wind. (18), the cart tracks straight down long aisles without constant wrist corrections, yet pivots instantly when nudged sideways.

That helpful geometry becomes sensitive to dirt, however. Hair, string, or flat spots worn into polyurethane rubber by rough parking-lot asphalt can throw one front wheel slightly out of balance, triggering rapid side-to-side flutter at walking speed. (19), larger stores install magnetic wheel locks and smoother entryway pavers to keep carts off gritty curbs.

Next time a cart turns smoothly past a pyramid of apples, credit (20).

passage.title: Why Supermarket Shopping Carts Have Slightly Angled Front Casters
passage.text:
Push an empty shopping cart across a smooth supermarket floor, and it glides effortlessly around tight dairy corners with one hand. Try steering a heavy four-wheeled warehouse dolly whose wheels are all locked straight, by contrast, and turning requires lifting one end off the ground. Behind the shopping cart's nimble handling—and its occasional annoying wobble—lies subtle caster-wheel geometry.

A shopping cart pairs two fixed rear wheels with two front "swivel casters" that rotate 360 degrees. Look closely at a front wheel fork, and you will see the wheel axle sits a couple of centimeters BEHIND the vertical pivot pin attached to the cart frame. Engineers call that small offset "caster trail." Whenever you push the cart forward, floor friction pulls the wheel neatly into alignment behind the pivot, much like a weathervane aligning with the wind. (18), the cart tracks straight down long aisles without constant wrist corrections, yet pivots instantly when nudged sideways.

That helpful geometry becomes sensitive to dirt, however. Hair, string, or flat spots worn into polyurethane rubber by rough parking-lot asphalt can throw one front wheel slightly out of balance, triggering rapid side-to-side flutter at walking speed. (19), larger stores install magnetic wheel locks and smoother entryway pavers to keep carts off gritty curbs.

Next time a cart turns smoothly past a pyramid of apples, credit (20).
passage.translation: 滑らかなスーパーの床で空の買い物カートを押すと、乳製品売り場の狭い角でも片手で軽々と曲がれます。対照的に4輪とも向きが固定された重い倉庫台車を曲げようとすれば片側を持ち上げなければなりません。買い物カートの軽快な操作性（と時に起きる厄介なガタつき）の背後には繊細なキャスター車輪の幾何学があります。カートは固定された後輪2つと360度回転する前輪「自在キャスター」2つを組み合わせていますが、前輪をよく見ると車軸がフレームの垂直回転軸より数センチ「後ろ」にずらして配置されています。技術者が「キャスタートレイル」と呼ぶこのわずかなずれにより、前に押すだけで床の摩擦が車輪を風見鶏のように自然と進行方向へ揃えてくれます。(18)、長い通路では手首で微調整しなくてもまっすぐ進み、横へ軽く押せば瞬時に向きを変えられます。ただし髪の毛や糸くずの絡まり、駐車場の粗いアスファルトによる偏摩耗があると歩行速度で小刻みな横揺れが起きやすくなるため、(19)、大型店では駐車場の縁石乗り上げを防ぐ磁気ロックや滑らかな入口舗装を取り入れています。リンゴの山積みの横を滑らかに曲がれるのは(20)のおかげなのです。

passage.title: How Oyster Reefs Clean Estuaries and Buffer Storm Waves
passage.text:
Mention coral reefs, and people immediately picture colorful tropical lagoons teeming with fish. Along cooler, murkier river mouths from Tokyo Bay and Chesapeake Bay to the North Sea, another reef builder once shaped coastlines on an equally vast scale: the humble oyster. Historical harbor charts from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries show dense oyster beds rising meters thick across muddy estuaries—until heavy dredging and industrial pollution wiped out over eighty percent of them globally.

Marine restoration teams are now rebuilding oyster reefs not for seafood harvests, but for water quality and coastal defense. A single adult oyster pumps up to a hundred liters of murky water across its gills every day, filtering out excess microscopic algae fueled by farm and city runoff. Clearer water allows sunlight to reach seafloor eelgrass beds again, reviving oxygen levels and young flounder nurseries. (21), nitrogen locked into oyster shells and sediment no longer triggers suffocating summer "dead zones."

Oyster reefs act as living breakwaters too. As generations of new spat cement their rough shells atop older ones, the jagged calcium-carbonate ridge breaks incoming storm waves before they erode salt marshes and waterfront roads. Concrete seawalls crack and sink over decades, whereas a healthy oyster reef grows upward naturally to match rising sea levels. (22), volunteers collect clean discarded restaurant shells in mesh bags to give baby oysters hard surfaces to settle on.

Bringing filter-feeding shellfish back to urban bays demonstrates how nature-based restoration can (23).
passage.translation: サンゴ礁と聞けば誰もが熱帯のカラフルな海を思い浮かべますが、東京湾やチェサピーク湾、北海などの涼しく濁りのある河口域でも、かつて同じほど壮大な規模で海岸線を形作っていた礁の建築家がいました。カキ（牡蠣）です。17〜18世紀の海図には河口を何メートルもの厚さで覆うカキ礁が記されていましたが、乱獲と産業汚染で世界の8割以上が失われました。いま海洋再生チームは食用ではなく「水質浄化と海岸防災」のためにカキ礁を再生させています。成体のカキ1個は毎日最大100リットルの濁った水をエラに通して過剰な植物プランクトンをろ過し、透明度が戻ることで海底のアマモ場に光が届き稚魚のゆりかごが復活します。(21)、栄養塩の過剰による夏の酸欠海域（デッドゾーン）も抑えられます。さらに世代を重ねて殻が固着したギザギザの礁は生きた防波堤となり、コンクリート護岸と違って海面上昇に合わせ自ら上へと成長します。(22)、ボランティアは飲食店から集めた清潔なカキ殻を網袋に詰め、幼生が付着する足場を作っています。都市の湾に二枚貝を取り戻す試みは、自然を活かした再生がいかに(23)かを示しています。

passage.title: Submitting Slides Before the History Symposium
passage.text:
From: Organizing Desk, Regional High School History Symposium
To: Presenting Student Teams
Subject: Font-embedding rule and Tuesday upload deadline

Dear presenting teams,
We are looking forward to hearing your twelve-minute research presentations at Civic Auditorium next Saturday! Because sixteen schools are presenting back-to-back in one afternoon, participants will NOT connect personal laptops or tablets at the podium; all slides will run from a single auditorium Windows PC.

Please export your presentation in BOTH PowerPoint (.pptx) and PDF formats and upload them to our symposium folder by 5:00 p.m. on Tuesday. Decorative fonts downloaded on home Macs or iPads often vanish or scramble line breaks on another computer—check "Embed fonts in file" when saving, or stick to standard system fonts, and verify your PDF backup carefully.

Video clips must be embedded directly inside the slide file rather than linked to YouTube, as auditorium Wi-Fi is turned off during sessions.

Symposium Technical Team

passage.title: Distinguishing "Social Jetlag" from Sleep Debt
passage.text:
Most high schoolers and office workers know the groggy feeling of short weekday sleep, and many try to make up for six-hour weeknights by sleeping until eleven a.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. Catching extra rest certainly feels refreshing on Sunday afternoon. Yet chronobiologists—researchers who study the body's twenty-four-hour circadian clocks—have found that swinging wildly between early weekday alarms and late weekend sleep-ins creates a hidden disruption they call "social jetlag."

Every organ in the human body, from liver enzymes and gut bacteria to blood-pressure hormones, runs on daily timing cues coordinated by a master clock in the brain's hypothalamus. That master clock calibrates itself primarily by when bright morning light first hits the retina. Stay up until two a.m. on Friday and Saturday and draw the curtains until noon, and your biological clock shifts roughly two to three hours westward—essentially flying your internal organs from Tokyo to Bangkok for the weekend.

When Monday's six-thirty alarm rings, forcing yourself out of bed does not snap those internal clocks back into place immediately; the pancreas and digestive tract may still expect midnight rest while you eat breakfast. Epidemiological studies tracking thousands of adults and teens show that even among people who average seven and a half hours of sleep per night across the week, a weekend midpoint shift of two hours or more correlates with foggier Monday memory, mood dips, and poorer blood-sugar regulation.

Sleep clinicians do not advise exhausted students to forfeit rest altogether, of course. Rather than sleeping until noon, they recommend anchoring wake-up times within sixty to ninety minutes of weekday schedules, stepping into outdoor daylight right after rising, and taking a brief twenty-minute early-afternoon nap if needed.

Consistent rhythm, it turns out, nourishes the brain nearly as much as total hours on the pillow.

Those whose weekend sleep shifted by two or more hours still showed Monday memory fog and poorer metabolic control.
Sleeping until noon on Sunday doubled math test scores.

items.translation: 週平均で7時間半眠っている人たちの間でも、どのような注目すべき調査結果が出ましたか。

Set alarms two hours earlier on Sunday than on Tuesday.
Stay indoors behind dark curtains until four p.m.
Take a four-hour nap from six p.m. to ten p.m.

items.prompt: Because river ice breaks up unpredictably in late March, kayak rentals remain (     ) until harbor patrol boats clear the channel.
items.explanation: 3月下旬は川氷が予測しがたく割れるため、巡視艇が水路の安全を確認するまでカヤック貸出は「一時停止された」状態のままであるremain suspended。
distractorReasons: surroundは取り囲む。
suspectは疑う。
sustainは維持する（untilとの論理が逆）。
suspend service/rentalsで貸出や業務を一時中止する。
items.translation: 3月下旬は川の氷がいつ割れるか予測できないため、港の巡視艇が水路の安全を確認するまでカヤックの貸出は休止されています。

items.prompt: Although the two violin bows weighed almost the same, the concertmaster noticed an (     ) improvement in bounce and tone with the older stick.
items.explanation: 重さはほぼ同じだったにもかかわらず、コンサートマスターは古い弓のほうが跳ね返りや音色に「非常に大きな・計り知れない」向上があることに気づいたimmense improvement。
distractorReasons: imaginaryは架空の。
immense improvementで非常に大きな改善。Althoughの対比と合致。
impartialは公平な。
immatureは未熟な。
items.translation: その2本のバイオリンの弓は重さがほぼ同じでしたが、コンサートマスターは古い弓のほうが弾みと音色が格段に優れていることに気づきました。

items.prompt: To stop coastal dunes from blowing onto the railway tracks, volunteers spent Saturday morning (     ) native beach grass along the ridge.
items.explanation: 海岸砂丘の砂が線路へ吹き込むのを防ぐため、砂丘の尾根に沿って在来の海浜植物の苗を「移植する・植え替える」作業を行ったtransplanting。
distractorReasons: translateは翻訳する。
transmitは信号や病気を伝える。
transplant seedlings/grassで植物を移植する。
transformは変形させる（along the ridgeと組んで植栽動作を表すのはtransplanting）。
items.translation: 海岸の砂丘から線路へ砂が吹き込むのを防ぐため、ボランティアは土曜の午前中をかけて砂丘の背に在来の海浜草を植えつけました。

items.prompt: All overnight freight trains were routed around the valley (     ) rockfall inspections inside the north tunnel.
items.explanation: 北トンネル内の落石点検「のために・が理由で」夜間貨物列車はすべて谷を迂回して運行されたon account of。

by means ofは〜という手段で。
in favor ofは〜に賛成して。
on behalf ofは〜を代表して。
items.translation: 北トンネル内で落石点検が行われたため、夜間の貨物列車はすべて谷を迂回するルートに変更されました。

items.prompt: Before returning borrowed brass instruments at graduation, band seniors have every valve and slide professionally (     ).
items.explanation: 卒業時に借用していた金管楽器を返却する前に、すべてのピストンと抜き差し管を専門職人に「整備・点検手入れしてもらう」have ... serviced。

surviveは生き残る。
surveyは調査・測量する。
have an instrument/car servicedで専門家に整備・メンテナンスしてもらう。
items.translation: 卒業時に借りていた金管楽器を返却する前に、吹奏楽部の3年生はすべてのバルブとスライドを専門店で整備してもらいます。

items.prompt: Pediatricians are increasingly (     ) about energy drinks marketed to middle schoolers because caffeine disrupts adolescent deep sleep.
items.explanation: カフェインが思春期の深い睡眠を妨げるため、中学生向けエナジードリンクに対して小児科医たちはますます「声高に意見を述べる・積極的に警鐘を鳴らす」ようになっているvocal about ...。
distractorReasons: be vocal about ... で…について率直・積極的に声を上げる。
vacantは空いている。
vagueは曖昧な。
vainは無駄な・うぬぼれた。
items.translation: カフェインが十代の深い睡眠を妨げるため、中学生向けに宣伝されるエナジードリンクに対して小児科医たちはますます強く警鐘を鳴らすようになっています。

items.prompt: Installing rubber pads beneath the rooftop heat pump brought welcome (     ) to tenants sleeping on the top floor.
items.explanation: 屋上ヒートポンプの下に防振ゴムパッドを敷いたことで、最上階で眠る入居者に喜ばしい「静けさ・平穏」がもたらされたquietude。
distractorReasons: resentmentは憤慨。
quietudeは静寂・穏やかさ。rooftop heat pumpの防振対策と合致。
reluctanceは気乗りしないこと。
quarrelは口論。
items.translation: 屋上のヒートポンプの下に防振ゴムパッドを設置したことで、最上階で眠る入居者たちにありがたい静けさが戻りました。

items.prompt: Had the ferry captain ignored the sudden drop in barometer readings, the vessel (     ) been caught in gale-force crosswinds offshore.
items.explanation: 過去の事実に反する仮定Had S + p.p.（もし船長が気圧急降下を無視していたら）の帰結節なのでmight have been caught（仮定法過去完了）。
distractorReasons: will haveは直説法未来完了。
hasでは仮定法過去完了にならない。

may + beenは文法的に不可。
items.translation: もしフェリーの船長が気圧計の急な低下を無視していたら、船は沖合で暴風並みの横風に巻き込まれていたかもしれません。

passage.title: Why Bridges Have Finger-Shaped Metal Joints
passage.text:
Drive or cycle across a long river bridge, and you will occasionally hear a rhythmic double thump beneath your tires while passing over a row of interlocking steel "fingers" set flush into the asphalt. Commuters rarely give those toothed metal plates a second glance, yet without expansion joints spaced carefully along the deck, a steel or concrete bridge would literally tear itself apart within a single year of seasonal weather.

Solid as bridge girders appear, every span behaves like a giant thermometer. On a freezing January midnight and a blazing August afternoon, a three-hundred-meter steel bridge can shrink and lengthen by more than fifteen centimeters as metal atoms vibrate faster in the heat. If engineers bolted both ends rigidly into concrete abutments, summer expansion would buckle the roadway upward, while winter contraction would crack supporting piers. (18), leaving a plain open slot wide enough to absorb fifteen centimeters of movement would create a dangerous trench capable of trapping bicycle wheels and jarring car suspensions.

Interlocking finger joints solve both problems elegantly. Two heavy steel plates cast with long tapered teeth are anchored to opposite deck sections so their fingers slide smoothly past one another as the bridge breathes in and out. Even when the gap opens widest in midwinter, vehicle tires roll continuously across overlapping steel teeth rather than dropping into a void. (19), rubber drainage troughs slung underneath catch salty slush and grit before runoff can rust structural bearings below.

Next time tires click softly over a bridge deck, that brief sound marks hardware that (20).
passage.translation: 長い川の橋を車や自転車で渡ると、アスファルトと同じ高さに埋め込まれた鋼鉄の「指」が噛み合う継ぎ目の上でタイヤがリズミカルにトン、トンと鳴ることがあります。普段は気にも留めない金属板ですが、この伸縮装置がなければ鋼橋やコンクリート橋は1年の寒暖差だけで自壊してしまいます。長さ300メートルの鋼橋は真冬の深夜と真夏の午後とで15センチ以上も伸縮するため、両端を橋台に完全固定すれば夏は路面が盛り上がり冬は橋脚にひびが入ります。(18)、15センチの隙間をただ開けておけば自転車の車輪が落ちる危険な溝になってしまいます。噛み合わせ式のフィンガージョイントは両側の桁に細長い鋼の歯を互い違いに配置し、冬に最も隙間が開いてもタイヤが途切れず歯の上を渡れるようにしています。(19)、下に吊られたゴム製の排水樋が融雪塩を含んだ泥水を受け止め、下の支承が錆びるのを防ぎます。タイヤの軽い通過音は、(20)装置が働いている証しなのです。

passage.title: How Rooftop Solar Panels Pair Well with Meadows
passage.text:
For years, architects designing flat commercial roofs treated green roofs and solar panels as competing choices: an owner could either lay trays of drought-hardy sedum plants to absorb stormwater or bolt down racks of photovoltaic modules to generate clean electricity. Across Germany, Switzerland, and Japan, however, building scientists are increasingly combining both systems into "biosolar" rooftops—discovering that plants and silicon cells actually help each other perform better.

A bare black waterproof membrane on a sunny July roof can easily bake at sixty-five degrees Celsius. Counterintuitively, solar panels lose electrical efficiency once their cells heat much above twenty-five degrees, dropping output just when afternoon air conditioners demand maximum power. When low-growing native wildflowers and mosses carpet the soil beneath raised panel frames, moisture evaporating gently from leaves cools the surrounding air by several degrees. (21), panels hovering overhead stay cooler and generate up to five percent more summer electricity than identical arrays mounted over bare gravel or tar.

The partnership works just as generously in reverse. Unshaded rooftop gardens often scorch into uniform mats of tough succulents, leaving little variety for urban insects. Angled solar frames create a patchwork of sunny strips, dappled shade, and rain-drip lines across the soil bed. (22), dozens of wildflower species bloom in staggered waves from April through October, feeding solitary bees and hoverflies high above busy streets.

Provided roof beams are engineered for wet soil weight, pairing greenery with solar arrays turns idle rooftops into (23).
passage.translation: 長年、商業ビルの陸屋根設計では「屋上緑化」と「太陽光パネル」は二者択一だと考えられてきました。しかし現在、ドイツやスイス、日本では両者を組み合わせる「バイオソーラー（緑化一体型太陽光）」屋上が広がり、植物と太陽電池が互いの性能を高め合うことが分かっています。真夏の黒い防水シート上は65度にも達しますが、太陽電池は25度を大きく超えると発電効率が落ちる弱点があります。架台の下に背の低い在来草花やコケを植えると葉の蒸散で周囲の空気が数度冷やされ、(21)、裸の砂利や防水層の上より夏の発電量が最大5％向上します。逆方向の恩恵も大きく、日陰のない屋上緑化は乾燥に強い多肉植物ばかりになりがちですが、傾斜したパネルが日向と木漏れ日、雨だれの変化をつくるため、(22)、春から秋まで多様な野花が咲き継ぎハチやヒラタアブを養います。湿った土の荷重に耐える構造設計さえ整えば、この組み合わせは屋上を(23)へと変えてくれます。

passage.title: Preparing Pottery Pieces for the Raku Firing Day
passage.text:
From: Ceramics Club Advisor, Makoto Hori
To: All Registered Raku Workshop Potters
Subject: Clay choice and dress rules for Saturday's outdoor raku firing

Hello everyone,
Our outdoor raku firing behind the art studio is set for this Saturday from 9:30 a.m. Unlike ordinary electric kiln firings that cool slowly overnight, raku pieces are lifted red-hot from the gas kiln at nine hundred degrees with long iron tongs and placed straight into metal bins filled with dry sawdust.

Because of that extreme thermal shock, bowls thrown from smooth porcelain clay will shatter almost immediately. Every piece you bring on Saturday must already be bisque-fired using coarse grogged raku clay, whose tiny pre-fired sand particles open microscopic pathways for steam and heat to escape safely. Maximum height is eighteen centimeters so four pots fit per load.

For safety around glowing tongs and smoke, synthetic fleece jackets and nylon running shoes are not allowed near the kiln pad; please wear long-sleeved cotton denim, leather closed-toe shoes, and hair ties.

Makoto Hori
passage.translation: 陶芸部顧問の堀誠先生から楽焼（らくやき）実習参加者へのメール。今週土曜午前9時半から美術室裏で屋外の楽焼焼成を行う。一晩かけてゆっくり冷ます通常の電気窯とは異なり、楽焼では900度に赤熱した器を長い鉄ばさみでガス窯から直接取り出し、乾いたおがくず入りの金属缶へ入れる。急激な熱衝撃がかかるため、滑らかな磁器土で作った茶碗はほぼ確実に割れてしまう。土曜に持参する作品はすべて、微細な焼き砂（シャモット）を含み蒸気や熱を逃がしやすい粗めの楽焼用粘土で素焼き済みのものに限る（1回に4点入るよう高さ18センチ以内）。安全のため化学繊維のフリースやナイロン靴は窯場近くで禁止とし、綿デニムの長袖、つま先の覆われた革靴、髪留めを着用すること。

items.prompt: Why must participants use coarse grogged raku clay rather than smooth porcelain clay?
choices: Porcelain clay melts iron tongs at room temperature.
Tiny sand particles in grogged clay let steam and heat escape without shattering the pot.
Grogged clay turns bright blue without glaze.
Grogged clay requires no bisque firing beforehand.
items.explanation: smooth porcelain clay will shatter almost immediately ... coarse grogged raku clay, whose tiny pre-fired sand particles open microscopic pathways for steam and heat to escape safelyとある。
distractorReasons: 常温で鉄ばさみが溶けることはない。
砂粒（シャモット）が蒸気と熱の逃げ道をつくり急冷時の破損を防ぐため。
釉薬なしで青くなる話ではない。
素焼き不要とは逆（already be bisque-firedが必要）。
items.translation: 滑らかな磁器土ではなく粗めのシャモット入り楽焼粘土を使わなければならないのはなぜですか。
